title: Angara v. Electoral Commission
summary: The Supreme Court affirmed its power of judicial review, holding that the judiciary is the final arbiter of constitutional disputes. The Electoral Commission has exclusive jurisdiction over election contests of legislative members.
doctrine: The Supreme Court has the power of judicial review — the authority to determine whether acts of the legislature or executive are in accordance with the Constitution.
fullText:
LAUREL, J.:

This is an original action instituted in this court by the petitioner, Jose A. Angara, for the issuance of a writ of prohibition to restrain and inhibit the Electoral Commission from taking further cognizance of the protest filed by Pedro Ynsua against the election of said petitioner as member of the National Assembly for the first assembly district of the Province of Tayabas.

The Constitution is a definition of the powers of government. Who is to determine the nature, scope and extent of such powers? The Constitution itself has provided for the instrumentality of the judiciary as the rational way. And when the judiciary mediates to allocate constitutional boundaries, it does not assert any superiority over the other departments; it does not in reality nullify or invalidate an act of the legislature, but only asserts the solemn and sacred obligation assigned to it by the Constitution to determine conflicting claims of authority under the Constitution and to establish for the parties in an actual controversy the rights which that instrument secures and guarantees to them.

The government established by the Constitution follows fundamentally the theory of separation of powers into the legislative, the executive and the judicial. The Constitution has blocked out with deft strokes and in bold lines, allotment of power to the executive, the legislative and the judicial departments of the government.

title: Villavicencio v. Lukban
summary: The Mayor of Manila forcibly deported 170 women to Davao without their consent. The Supreme Court held this was an unlawful exercise of police power and a violation of the constitutional right to liberty and freedom of movement.
doctrine: No law, no matter how broadly worded, authorizes the deportation of citizens within the country without due process. Police power cannot be exercised in a manner that violates fundamental civil liberties.
fullText:
MALCOLM, J.:

The annals of juridical history fail to reveal a case quite as remarkable as the one which this application for habeas corpus brings up for decision. While hardly combating the right of the courts to grant the writ of habeas corpus in a proper case, respondents vigorously resist the issuance of the writ to any of the women.

The Mayor of the City of Manila, Justo Lukban, for the best of all reasons, to extinguish vice in Manila, ordered the segregated district for women of ill repute closed. Between October 16 and 25, 1918, the women were placed on board the steamers and sent to Davao. The women were not asked if they wished to depart from Manila. They had no opportunity to collect their belongings or to settle their affairs. They were compelled to go.

Law defines power. Centuries ago Magna Charta laid down the principle that no freeman shall be taken, or imprisoned, or disseized, or outlawed, or banished, or in any way destroyed, nor will the King go upon him, nor send upon him, except by the legal judgment of his peers or by the law of the land. No official, no matter how high, is above the law.

title: Marcos v. Manglapus
summary: The Supreme Court upheld President Aquino's decision to bar the return of former President Marcos to the Philippines, ruling that the President has residual powers to protect national interest and maintain peace and order, even if such power is not expressly granted by the Constitution.
doctrine: The President has unstated residual powers which are implied from the grant of executive power and necessary for her to comply with her duties under the Constitution. The right to travel may be impaired in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health.
fullText:
CORTES, J.:

This case involves a petition for mandamus and prohibition asking the Court to order the respondents to issue travel documents to Mr. Marcos and the immediate members of his family and to enjoin the implementation of the President's decision to bar their return to the Philippines.

The issue is basically one of power: whether or not, in the exercise of the powers granted by the Constitution, the President may prohibit the Marcoses from returning to the Philippines.

According to the 1987 Constitution, the executive power shall be vested in the President. The powers of the President cannot be said to be limited only to the specific powers enumerated in the Constitution. Residual power, the power of the President as the head of state, is the power to protect the general welfare of the people. It is founded on the duty of the President, as steward of the people.

title: People v. Marti
summary: The Bill of Rights protection against unreasonable searches and seizures applies only against the government and its agents. Evidence obtained through a search by a private individual (shipping company employee) is admissible even without a warrant.
doctrine: The constitutional protection against unreasonable searches and seizures refers to the immunity of one's person from interference by government. It cannot be extended to acts committed by private individuals so as to bring it within the ambit of alleged unlawful intrusion by the government.
fullText:
BIDIN, J.:

This is an appeal from the decision of the Regional Trial Court convicting accused-appellant of violation of the Dangerous Drugs Act. The appellant contends that the evidence was obtained through an illegal search.

The package containing marijuana was voluntarily opened by the employee of a private shipping company in the regular course of business. The constitutional proscription against unlawful searches and seizures therefore finds no application. The constitutional protection guarantees the right of the people to be secure in their persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures.

The protection is against the State — against the government and its agencies. It is not meant to be invoked against acts of private individuals. The Bill of Rights governs the relationship between the individual and the state.

title: Oposa v. Factoran
summary: Minor children, represented by their parents, filed a class suit to cancel all existing timber license agreements. The Court recognized their legal standing based on the concept of intergenerational responsibility, holding that every generation has a responsibility to preserve the environment for future generations.
doctrine: The right to a balanced and healthful ecology is a self-executory constitutional right that does not need enabling legislation. Present generations have the obligation to preserve the environment for future generations (intergenerational equity).
fullText:
DAVIDE, JR., J.:

In a broader sense, this petition bears upon the right of Filipinos to a balanced and healthful ecology which the petitioners dramatically associate with the twin concepts of inter-generational responsibility and inter-generational justice.

The petitioners, all minors duly represented by their parents, institute this action as a class suit. Their personality to sue in behalf of the succeeding generations can only be based on the concept of intergenerational responsibility insofar as the right to a balanced and healthful ecology is concerned.

The right to a balanced and healthful ecology carries with it the correlative duty to refrain from impairing the environment. This right implies the judicious disposition, utilization, management, renewal and conservation of the country's forest, mineral, land, waters, fisheries, wildlife, offshore areas, and other natural resources.

title: Estrada v. Sandiganbayan
summary: Former President Estrada challenged the constitutionality of the Plunder Law (RA 7080) as vague and overbroad. The Supreme Court upheld its constitutionality, ruling that the law provides sufficient standards and does not violate due process.
doctrine: The Plunder Law is not unconstitutionally vague. A statute is not rendered uncertain and void merely because general terms are used, or because of the employment of terms without defining them. The void-for-vagueness doctrine applies only in free speech cases.
fullText:
BELLOSILLO, J.:

Petitioner Joseph Ejercito Estrada challenges the constitutionality of RA 7080, the Plunder Law, on the grounds that it is vague and violates due process.

The void-for-vagueness doctrine states that a statute which either forbids or requires the doing of an act in terms so vague that men of common intelligence must necessarily guess at its meaning and differ as to its application, violates the first essential of due process of law. However, the Court has consistently held that this doctrine applies only to free speech cases.

Congress is not restricted in the form of expression of its will, and its inability to so define the words employed in a statute will not necessarily result in the vagueness or ambiguity of the law so long as the legislative will is clear.

title: David v. Macapagal-Arroyo
summary: The Supreme Court declared Presidential Proclamation 1017 (state of national emergency) as constitutional in part but struck down the warrantless arrests and takeover of media facilities as unconstitutional, ruling that the President's calling-out power does not include the power to take over private utilities or media.
doctrine: The President's power to call out the armed forces does not include authority to take over privately-owned utilities or media. Emergency powers under Section 17, Article XII require delegation by Congress.
fullText:
SANDOVAL-GUTIERREZ, J.:

These seven consolidated petitions question the constitutionality of Presidential Proclamation No. 1017 (PP 1017) issued by President Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo on February 24, 2006, declaring a state of national emergency.

The Court rules that PP 1017 is constitutional insofar as it constitutes a call by the President for the AFP to prevent or suppress lawless violence. However, the provisions giving the President express or implied power to take over privately-owned public utility or business affected with public interest and to direct the AFP to enforce obedience to all laws are unconstitutional.

The President's calling-out power is exclusive to the President. The power to take over is a legislative power which Congress may delegate to the President only in times of war or other national emergency.

title: Republic v. Sandiganbayan
summary: The Republic sought to recover ill-gotten wealth allegedly acquired by cronies of former President Marcos. The Court established standards for recovery proceedings, distinguishing between civil forfeiture and criminal prosecution.
doctrine: Civil forfeiture proceedings for ill-gotten wealth are independent of criminal proceedings. The State need only prove by preponderance of evidence that the wealth was acquired through improper use of government power.
fullText:
CARPIO, J.:

This case involves the recovery by the Republic of the Philippines of ill-gotten wealth amassed by close associates of former President Ferdinand E. Marcos during his administration.

The 1987 Constitution expressly mandates the recovery of ill-gotten wealth. Executive Order Nos. 1 and 2, issued by President Corazon C. Aquino, created the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) to recover all ill-gotten wealth accumulated by former President Marcos, his immediate family, relatives, subordinates, and close associates.

Civil actions for recovery of ill-gotten wealth are entirely different from criminal actions for violations of the Anti-Graft Law. The quantum of proof required is only preponderance of evidence, not proof beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Manila Prince Hotel v. GSIS
summary: In the bidding for Manila Hotel shares, the Court upheld the Filipino First Policy provision of the Constitution, ruling that qualified Filipinos must be given preference in the grant of rights over natural resources and operation of public utilities.
doctrine: Section 10, Article XII of the Constitution (Filipino First Policy) is a mandatory, positive command which is complete in itself and needs no further guidelines or implementing laws to enforce it. Qualified Filipinos shall be preferred over foreign investors.
fullText:
BELLOSILLO, J.:

The Manila Hotel has been identified with the Filipino nation and has hosted many significant events in Philippine history. It is a proud legacy of our people. The controversy arises from the privatization of the Manila Hotel Corporation.

The Filipino First Policy enshrined in the 1987 Constitution mandates that in the grant of rights, privileges, and concessions covering the national economy and patrimony, the State shall give preference to qualified Filipinos. This is not merely a statement of principle; it is a mandatory positive command.

The Court holds that the Constitution should be interpreted in favor of Filipino interests. Section 10, Article XII is self-executing and does not require enabling legislation to be operative.

title: Tanada v. Tuvera
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that all laws must be published in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation before they can take effect. Without publication, no law or regulation can be enforced against the people.
doctrine: Publication is indispensable for the effectivity of laws. All statutes, presidential decrees, executive orders, proclamations, letters of instructions, and other presidential issuances with general applicability must be published before they become effective.
fullText:
CRUZ, J.:

This is a landmark case on the requirement of publication of laws before they can take effect. The petitioners seek a writ of mandamus to compel respondent public officials to publish various presidential decrees and other presidential issuances.

Article 2 of the Civil Code provides that laws shall take effect after fifteen days following the completion of their publication in the Official Gazette, unless it is otherwise provided. Publication is necessary to apprise the public of the contents of regulations and make people aware of what they must comply with.

The clear object of the law is to give the general public adequate notice of the various laws which are to regulate their actions and conduct as citizens. Without such notice and publication, there would be no basis for the application of the maxim 'ignorantia legis non excusat.'

title: Carino v. Insular Government
summary: An Igorot chief claimed ownership of ancestral land based on possession since time immemorial. The US Supreme Court (reviewing the Philippine SC) recognized native title, holding that long possession by indigenous peoples creates a presumption of ownership even without formal title.
doctrine: Native title or ownership of land by Filipinos by virtue of possession under a claim of ownership since time immemorial is recognized. Long-continued possession under claim of ownership creates a presumption that the land had never been part of the public domain.
fullText:
HOLMES, J. (US Supreme Court):

The petitioner, an Igorot of Benguet, claims that he and his ancestors have held the land in question as owners for more than 50 years before the Spanish conquest. The case presents a question of title to land in the Philippine Islands.

Whatever the law upon these points may be, and we mean to go no further than is necessary for decision, every presumption of ownership is in favor of one actually occupying land for the period prescribed. The Organic Act of July 1, 1902, made a rule of property in favor of Filipinos who had held land under a claim of ownership for the period prescribed.

It would be going too far to deny all rights to the inhabitants of the Philippines who had been in occupation of their land from time immemorial simply because the Spanish Government had not issued them a formal title.

title: People v. Echegaray
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of RA 7659 reimposing the death penalty, ruling that it does not constitute cruel, degrading, or inhuman punishment. The Congress has the power to impose the death penalty for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes.
doctrine: The death penalty per se is not cruel, degrading, or inhuman punishment. The 1987 Constitution did not abolish the death penalty outright but merely suspended its imposition, giving Congress the authority to reimpose it for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes.
fullText:
PER CURIAM:

The constitutionality of Republic Act No. 7659, reimposing the death penalty for certain heinous crimes, is challenged in this case.

The 1987 Constitution does not per se prohibit the imposition of the death penalty. Article III, Section 19(1) provides: 'Excessive fines shall not be imposed, nor cruel, degrading or inhuman punishment inflicted. Neither shall death penalty be imposed, unless, for compelling reasons involving heinous crimes, the Congress hereafter provides for it.'

The framers of the Constitution were clearly aware that the reimposition of the death penalty was a possibility. The Constitution merely suspends the imposition of the death penalty but does not altogether abolish it. Congress was given the discretion to determine whether to reimpose the penalty, and it exercised this prerogative through RA 7659.

title: Pharmaceutical and Health Care Association of the Philippines v. Duque
petitioner: Pharmaceutical and Health Care Association of the Philippines
summary: The Court ruled on the validity of administrative orders regulating infant formula marketing. It upheld the government's police power to regulate commercial activities affecting public health, while striking down provisions that exceeded the scope of the enabling law.
doctrine: Administrative agencies cannot promulgate rules that exceed the scope of their statutory authority. While police power allows regulation of commercial activities affecting public health, administrative regulations must conform to the standards set by the enabling statute.
citedStatutes: International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes
fullText:
AUSTRIA-MARTINEZ, J.:

This petition challenges the constitutionality and legality of certain provisions of Administrative Order No. 2006-0012, the Revised Implementing Rules and Regulations of Executive Order No. 51 (the Milk Code).

The State has the power to regulate commercial activities that affect public health under the police power. However, administrative regulations must be within the scope of the authority granted by law. An administrative agency cannot amend an act of Congress, and rules that go beyond the terms of the statute are void.

The Court finds that certain provisions of the questioned administrative order exceed the regulatory authority granted by EO 51 and are therefore invalid.

title: Imbong v. Ochoa
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act (RH Law) in its main provisions but struck down eight specific provisions as unconstitutional, including those compelling health workers to refer patients for reproductive health procedures against their religious beliefs.
doctrine: The RH Law does not violate the right to life as it does not legalize abortion. However, provisions that compel medical practitioners to refer patients for procedures against their religious convictions violate the guarantee of religious freedom. The State may promote reproductive health without infringing on conscientious objection.
fullText:
MENDOZA, J.:

These consolidated petitions challenge the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 10354, otherwise known as the Responsible Parenthood and Reproductive Health Act of 2012 (RH Law).

The Court finds that the RH Law, in its main provisions, is not unconstitutional. It does not violate the right to life as it prohibits abortion and does not authorize the use of abortifacients. The law promotes responsible parenthood and reproductive health which are legitimate state interests.

However, certain provisions are struck down. Section 7, which mandates health care providers to refer patients seeking reproductive health procedures to another facility despite their conscientious objection, violates the constitutional guarantee of religious freedom. The freedom of religion is a fundamental right that must be respected even in the pursuit of legitimate state objectives.

title: Belgica v. Ochoa
summary: The Supreme Court declared the Priority Development Assistance Fund (PDAF) or 'pork barrel' system unconstitutional for violating the principles of separation of powers and non-delegability of legislative power. The system allowed legislators to exercise post-enactment authority over budget execution.
doctrine: The Congressional Pork Barrel (PDAF) is unconstitutional because it violates the separation of powers principle by allowing legislators to exercise post-enactment authority in budget execution, which is an executive function. Legislators' participation in the implementation of the budget after its enactment is a prohibited intrusion into executive prerogatives.
fullText:
PERLAS-BERNABE, J.:

These consolidated petitions challenge the constitutionality of the Pork Barrel System, which has been characterized as a political tool for the benefit of legislators rather than for public interest.

The Congressional Pork Barrel, under its current form and operation, crosses the line of constitutionality. It is unconstitutional because it violates the constitutional provisions on separation of powers and non-delegability of legislative power. Through the system, individual legislators are given post-enactment measures — the power to identify projects and direct funds after the General Appropriations Act is passed.

The Court holds that the separation of powers mandate requires that the authority to execute or implement the national budget belongs to the Executive branch. Any legislative interference in the execution of the budget violates this principle. The PDAF, as it operates, is essentially an encroachment by the legislature into the domain of the executive.

title: Aquino v. Municipality of Malay
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the authority of local government units to order the demolition of illegally constructed establishments in tourist areas to protect the environment. The LGU exercised valid police power despite the establishment's claim of vested property rights.
doctrine: Local government units may exercise police power to demolish illegal structures that threaten the environment. The right to property is not absolute and must yield to the demands of the common good as defined by the legislature and administrative agencies.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

This case involves the power of local government units to enforce environmental laws through the demolition of structures built without the necessary permits and clearances.

The Constitution authorizes local government units to exercise police power through their legislative bodies. The Local Government Code grants them the power to enact ordinances and enforce them through appropriate sanctions. This includes the power to order the closure and demolition of establishments that violate environmental laws.

Property rights are not absolute. When the use of property is injurious to the health, morals, or safety of the community, the State may validly regulate or even prohibit such use.

title: Lim v. Executive Secretary
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) between the Philippines and the United States. The VFA was deemed a valid executive agreement that did not require ratification as a treaty by the US Senate.
doctrine: The VFA is constitutional. The Philippines, as a sovereign state, may enter into agreements allowing foreign military forces to temporarily visit the country for joint military exercises. Such agreements do not constitute a derogation of sovereignty.
fullText:
PUNO, J.:

The constitutionality of the Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA) entered into between the Republic of the Philippines and the United States of America is the central issue in this case.

Section 25, Article XVIII of the 1987 Constitution provides that foreign military bases, troops, or facilities shall not be allowed in the Philippines except under a treaty duly concurred in by the Senate. The VFA received the concurrence of the Philippine Senate.

The VFA is not a basing agreement. It deals with the treatment of United States military and civilian personnel visiting the Philippines. The agreement governs the conditions under which US armed forces may be present in Philippine territory for joint military exercises and other approved activities.

title: Francisco v. House of Representatives
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the filing of a second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Davide within the same year was unconstitutional. The one-year bar provision in the Constitution prevents harassment through successive impeachment complaints.
doctrine: The one-year bar rule on impeachment under Section 3(5), Article XI of the Constitution means that no impeachment proceedings shall be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year. This is a constitutional safeguard against legislative harassment.
fullText:
CARPIO MORALES, J.:

The fundamental issue in this case is whether the filing of a second impeachment complaint against Chief Justice Hilario G. Davide, Jr. within one year from the filing of the first complaint is constitutional.

Section 3(5) of Article XI of the Constitution provides that no impeachment proceedings shall be initiated against the same official more than once within a period of one year. The framers of the Constitution intended this provision as a safeguard against the use of impeachment as a tool for political harassment.

The Court holds that the word 'initiate' means to file the complaint and take initial action on it. The second impeachment complaint was filed within the prohibited one-year period and is therefore unconstitutional.

title: Republic v. Bermudez-Lorino
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the requirements for declaring a marriage void on the ground of psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code. The incapacity must be grave, pre-existing, and incurable.
doctrine: Psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code must be characterized by gravity, juridical antecedence, and incurability. It must be more than mere difficulty, refusal, or neglect in the performance of marital obligations.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

This case involves a petition for declaration of nullity of marriage on the ground of psychological incapacity under Article 36 of the Family Code.

The Supreme Court has laid down definitive guidelines in interpreting and applying Article 36. Psychological incapacity must be characterized by (a) gravity — it must be serious enough to disable the party from assuming the essential obligations of marriage; (b) juridical antecedence — it must be rooted in the history of the party antedating the marriage; and (c) incurability — it must be incurable or, even if curable, the cure is beyond the means of the party involved.

Mere showing of irreconcilable differences and conflicting personalities does not constitute psychological incapacity.

title: Republic v. Court of Appeals (Molina)
summary: The Supreme Court laid down the 'Molina guidelines' — eight requisites for the declaration of nullity of marriage based on psychological incapacity. This became the landmark ruling that established the strict interpretation of Article 36 of the Family Code.
doctrine: The burden of proof belongs to the plaintiff to show the nullity of the marriage. The root cause of psychological incapacity must be medically or clinically identified, alleged in the complaint, proven by experts, and clearly explained in the decision. The incapacity must be proven to be existing at the time of the celebration of marriage.
fullText:
PANGANIBAN, J.:

This is a petition for review on certiorari seeking the reversal of a decision declaring a marriage null and void on the ground of psychological incapacity.

The Court hereby lays down the following guidelines in the interpretation and application of Article 36 of the Family Code:

(1) The burden of proof belongs to the plaintiff.
(2) The root cause of the psychological incapacity must be medically or clinically identified, alleged in the complaint, sufficiently proven by experts, and clearly explained in the decision.
(3) The incapacity must be proven to be existing at the time of the celebration of the marriage.
(4) Such incapacity must be clinically or medically permanent or incurable.
(5) Such illness must be grave enough to bring about the disability of the party to assume the essential obligations of marriage.
(6) The essential marital obligations must be embraced by Articles 68 to 71 of the Family Code.
(7) Interpretations given by the National Appellate Matrimonial Tribunal of the Catholic Church in the Philippines are given great respect.
(8) The trial court must order the prosecuting attorney or fiscal and the Solicitor General to appear as counsel for the state.

title: Estrada v. Desierto
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that President Estrada had constructively resigned from the presidency, and that President Arroyo's assumption of power was legitimate. The totality of prior, contemporaneous, and posterior facts and circumstances showed Estrada's intent to resign.
doctrine: Resignation can be inferred from the totality of prior, contemporaneous, and posterior acts. The President is deemed to have resigned when his acts demonstrate a clear intent to relinquish the position. The legitimacy of the successor President is upheld when succession follows constitutional processes.
fullText:
PUNO, J.:

The case at bar poses legal questions of first impression. Petitioner Joseph Ejercito Estrada challenges the legitimacy of the assumption as President of the Philippines by respondent Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo.

The issue of whether petitioner resigned from the presidency is a question of fact. Resignation is a factual question and its elements are: (1) intent to resign, and (2) acts of relinquishment. The totality of prior, contemporaneous and posterior facts and circumstantial evidence bearing material relevance on the issue must be considered.

The Court examines the events leading to the assumption of respondent. The acts of petitioner show that he intended to resign. He called for snap elections, negotiated a dignified exit, and left Malacañang Palace. The angst of petitioner was not that he was resigning but that his resignation was not being treated with dignity.

title: Serrano v. Gallant Maritime Services
summary: The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the clause in RA 8042 (Migrant Workers Act) that limited money claims of illegally dismissed overseas Filipino workers to three months' salary. The provision violated the equal protection clause by discriminating against OFWs with longer contracts.
doctrine: The clause in Section 10 of RA 8042 limiting the money claims of illegally dismissed OFWs to three months for every year of the unexpired term is unconstitutional for violating the equal protection and due process clauses. OFWs are entitled to the full amount of their salaries for the unexpired portion of their contracts.
fullText:
AUSTRIA-MARTINEZ, J.:

At the core of this case is the constitutionality of the last clause in the fifth paragraph of Section 10 of Republic Act No. 8042, which reads: 'or for three (3) months for every year of the unexpired term, whichever is less.'

The Court holds that this clause is unconstitutional for being violative of the equal protection clause of the Constitution. The classification of OFWs based on the length of their contracts is not germane to the purpose of the law. It creates an absurd situation where an OFW with a longer contract receives less compensation than one with a shorter contract when both are illegally dismissed.

The equal protection clause guarantees that all persons or things similarly situated should be treated alike, both as to rights conferred and responsibilities imposed.

title: Agabon v. NLRC
summary: The Supreme Court modified the doctrine in Serrano v. NLRC, ruling that where the dismissal is for a just cause but without procedural due process, the dismissal is valid but the employer must pay nominal damages for violation of the employee's right to due process.
doctrine: Where the dismissal is for just or authorized cause but due process was not observed, the dismissal remains valid. However, the employer shall indemnify the employee through payment of nominal damages for violation of procedural due process rights.
fullText:
YNARES-SANTIAGO, J.:

The pivotal question in this case is the effect of the employer's failure to comply with the requirements of due process in terminating the services of an employee for a just cause.

The Court abandons the ruling in Serrano v. NLRC that an employer who fails to comply with procedural due process must pay the employee back wages from the time of dismissal until the court finds that the dismissal was for a just cause. The better rule is that the dismissal should be upheld if a just cause exists, but the employer must be sanctioned for non-compliance with procedural requirements.

Nominal damages are awarded not as a penalty but as a vindication of the employee's right to due process. The amount shall be determined by the court based on the circumstances of each case.

title: Rubi v. Provincial Board of Mindoro
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the power of the provincial governor to require Mangyans (indigenous peoples) to live in reservations. The Court held that this was a valid exercise of police power aimed at advancing the welfare of non-Christian tribes, though the decision has been widely criticized.
doctrine: The State may exercise police power to segregate and resettle indigenous communities in the interest of their advancement and the general welfare. This case represents an early and controversial interpretation of police power in relation to indigenous rights.
fullText:
MALCOLM, J.:

This is an application for habeas corpus in favor of Rubi and other Manguianes (Mangyans) of the Province of Mindoro. It challenges the legality of the order of the provincial governor directing certain non-Christian inhabitants to establish their residence in a reservation.

Section 2145 of the Administrative Code provides: 'With the prior approval of the Department Head, the provincial governor of any province in which non-Christian inhabitants are found is authorized, when such a course is deemed necessary in the interest of law and order, to direct such inhabitants to take up their habitation on sites on unoccupied public lands to be selected by him.'

The Court upholds the constitutionality of this provision as a valid exercise of the police power. The State has the duty to promote the welfare of all its inhabitants, including those who are in a less advanced state of civilization.

title: Republic v. Hong Kong Special Administrative Region
summary: The Supreme Court modified the prevailing rule that bail is not a matter of right in extradition cases. The Court ruled that a potential extraditee may apply for bail, which may be granted if the extraditee can show by clear and convincing evidence that he is not a flight risk and will abide by the orders of the court.
doctrine: While the right to bail in extradition proceedings is not absolute, it is not entirely unavailable. A potential extraditee may apply for bail, which the court may grant on the basis of clear and convincing evidence that the applicant is not a flight risk and will comply with court orders.
fullText:
CALLEJO, SR., J.:

The issue before the Court is whether a potential extraditee is entitled to bail during the pendency of the extradition proceedings.

The Court modifies the prevailing jurisprudence that bail is not available in extradition proceedings. While extradition proceedings are not criminal in nature, the potential extraditee faces incarceration pending the resolution of the proceedings. The universal declaration of human rights recognizes the right to liberty and the right against arbitrary detention.

The Court holds that a potential extraditee may apply for bail. The applicant bears the burden of proving by clear and convincing evidence that he is not a flight risk, that there exist special humanitarian and compelling circumstances, and that he will abide by all orders and processes of the extradition court.

title: Ermita-Malate Hotel and Motel Operators Association v. City Mayor
petitioner: Ermita-Malate Hotel and Motel Operators Association
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of a Manila city ordinance imposing regulatory requirements on motels and hotels in the interest of public morals. The ordinance was a valid exercise of police power as it bore a reasonable relation to the legitimate governmental objective of curbing immorality.
doctrine: An ordinance regulating motels and hotels is a valid exercise of police power if it has a reasonable relationship to a legitimate governmental objective. The presumption is always in favor of the validity of a law, and the burden of proof is on those attacking its constitutionality.
fullText:
FERNANDO, J.:

The validity of an ordinance of the City of Manila, Ordinance No. 4760, regulating hotels, motels, and lodging houses in the city, is challenged in this case.

Police power is the most essential, insistent and illimitable of powers, extending as it does to all the great public needs. The presumption is towards the validity of a law. The courts will not strike down a law unless it clearly and unequivocally violates constitutional provisions.

The ordinance in question was enacted to minimize certain practices hurtful to public morals. There is a reasonable connection between the regulatory measures and the legislative purpose. The means employed are not unduly oppressive upon individuals.

title: Disini v. Secretary of Justice
summary: The Supreme Court upheld most provisions of the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 but struck down several provisions as unconstitutional, including the online libel provision insofar as it penalizes those who simply receive and react to libelous posts, and the provision authorizing the DOJ to restrict or block access to computer data.
doctrine: Online libel under the Cybercrime Prevention Act is not unconstitutional per se but is limited to the original author of the libelous post. The State cannot restrict internet content without judicial intervention. Real-time collection of traffic data requires a court warrant.
fullText:
ABAD, J.:

These consolidated petitions assail the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 10175, the Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012.

The Court upholds the constitutionality of Section 4(c)(4) on online libel insofar as it applies to the original author of the post. However, it is unconstitutional insofar as it penalizes those who simply receive the post and react to it. To penalize the receiver and reactor would have a chilling effect on freedom of expression.

Section 19 which authorizes the Department of Justice to restrict or block access to computer data is unconstitutional. Only a judicial authority can order the restriction of internet content. The provision constitutes a prior restraint on the right to freedom of expression.

title: White Light Corporation v. City of Manila
summary: The Supreme Court struck down a Manila city ordinance prohibiting short-time hotel admissions (wash-up rates), ruling that it was an unreasonable exercise of police power that unduly interfered with personal liberty and the right to privacy without sufficient justification.
doctrine: An ordinance that unreasonably restricts personal liberty in the guise of police power is unconstitutional. The right to liberty includes the right of individuals to make intimate personal choices. The means employed by the ordinance must have a reasonable relationship to its legitimate purpose.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

This case involves the constitutionality of Manila City Ordinance No. 7774, which prohibits short-time admission, short-time admission rates, and wash-up rate schemes in hotels, motels, and similar establishments.

Liberty in its broad sense is the right of individuals to be free to use their faculties in all lawful ways, to live and work where they will, to earn their livelihood by any lawful calling, and to pursue any livelihood or avocation. The ordinance in question infringes upon this broad concept of liberty.

While the police power of the State is broad enough to regulate businesses, the means employed must bear a reasonable relationship to the purpose of the regulation. The questioned ordinance fails this test. It employs a blunderbuss approach that overly restricts personal liberty when less intrusive means are available.

title: Javellana v. Executive Secretary
summary: The Supreme Court, in a controversial decision during martial law, ruled that the 1973 Constitution had been validly ratified through citizens' assemblies rather than a plebiscite. The decision also held that the question of the validity of the new Constitution was a political question beyond judicial review.
doctrine: The validity of the ratification of the Constitution is a political question that lies outside the ambit of judicial review. Once a new Constitution is in force and the people have acquiesced to it, the courts cannot declare it invalid.
fullText:
CONCEPCION, C.J.:

The question before the Court is whether the proposed 1973 Constitution has been validly ratified and is in force.

The Court is deeply divided on this issue. Six members hold that the 1973 Constitution has not been validly ratified. Four members maintain that it has been validly ratified. Two members hold that the question is political and therefore non-justiciable.

The Court declares that it cannot act on the cases because the political question doctrine bars judicial inquiry. The new Constitution is regarded as in force, there being no judicial obstacle to its effectivity. The Court takes note that the people have generally acquiesced to the new Constitution.

title: People v. Cayat
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of Act No. 1639 prohibiting non-Christian tribes from purchasing or consuming alcoholic beverages. The classification was deemed reasonable as it was based on substantial distinctions germane to the purpose of the law.
doctrine: The equal protection clause does not prohibit classification. A law is valid if: (1) the classification rests on substantial distinctions; (2) it is germane to the purpose of the law; (3) it is not limited to existing conditions only; and (4) it applies equally to all members of the same class.
fullText:
MORAN, J.:

The accused, a member of the non-Christian tribe of Benguet, was charged with violation of Act No. 1639 which prohibits any member of a non-Christian tribe from buying, receiving, or having in his possession any intoxicating liquor.

The guaranty of equal protection of the laws is not violated by legislation which applies only to those persons falling within a specified class, if it applies alike to all persons within such class and reasonable grounds exist for making a distinction between those who fall within the class and those who do not.

The classification between Christians and non-Christians is based upon real and substantial distinctions. The distinction is germane to the purpose of the law. The law was not made only for existing conditions. The act applies equally to all members of the class.

title: Chavez v. Gonzales
summary: The Supreme Court struck down government warnings against media from airing the 'Hello Garci' wiretapped conversations, ruling that they constituted prior restraint on press freedom. The Court reaffirmed that any system of prior restraints bears a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity.
doctrine: Any act of the government that restrains speech or press before publication is a prior restraint and bears a heavy presumption against constitutional validity. The government carries a heavy burden of justifying any system of prior restraint. Press freedom may only be restricted by subsequent punishment, not prior censorship.
fullText:
PUNO, C.J.:

This case involves the constitutionality of acts of the government restraining the media from airing or publishing the contents of wiretapped conversations purportedly between President Arroyo and a COMELEC commissioner.

Freedom of expression is the foundation of a free, open, and democratic society. It is an indispensable condition for nearly every other form of freedom. The First Amendment freedoms — of speech, press, religion, assembly — are ranked as preferred rights in our hierarchy of constitutional values.

Prior restraint refers to official governmental restrictions on the press or other forms of expression in advance of actual publication or dissemination. Any system of prior restraints comes to the Court bearing a heavy presumption against its constitutional validity. The government thus carries a heavy burden of showing justification for the enforcement of such a restraint.

title: Manotoc v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court laid down strict requirements for the validity of substituted service of summons, ruling that the sheriff must show impossibility of personal service and the substituted service must comply with statutory requirements to satisfy due process.
doctrine: Substituted service of summons is extraordinary in character and may be used only as prescribed and in the circumstances authorized by statute. The impossibility of personal service must be shown by stating the efforts made to find the defendant and the fact that such efforts were unsuccessful.
fullText:
SANDOVAL-GUTIERREZ, J.:

The question before the Court is the validity of the substituted service of summons effected upon the petitioner.

Section 6 of Rule 14 of the Rules of Court provides that service of summons shall be made by handing a copy thereof to the defendant in person, or, if he refuses to receive and sign for it, by tendering it to him. It is only when the defendant cannot be served personally within a reasonable time that substituted service may be made.

The sheriff's return must show that the defendant could not be served within a reasonable time, the efforts made to locate the defendant, and the person to whom the summons was served. Substituted service must strictly comply with these requirements as it is in derogation of the usual method of service.

title: Araullo v. Aquino
summary: The Supreme Court declared the Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP) unconstitutional insofar as it involved the cross-border transfers of savings and the withdrawal of unobligated allotments from implementing agencies. These acts violated the constitutional prohibition against unauthorized transfer of appropriations.
doctrine: The President's power to augment appropriations is limited to savings and cannot include unobligated allotments or unreleased appropriations. Cross-border transfers of appropriations — from one branch of government to another — violate the Constitution. Only the specific officials named in the Constitution may authorize augmentation from savings within their respective offices.
fullText:
BERSAMIN, J.:

These consolidated petitions assail the constitutionality of the Disbursement Acceleration Program (DAP) implemented by the Executive Department.

The power of the President to augment items in the General Appropriations Act is circumscribed by the Constitution. Section 25(5) of Article VI limits this power to augmentation of items in the General Appropriations Act from savings in other items of their respective appropriations.

The Court holds that the DAP violated the Constitution insofar as it authorized: (1) the withdrawal of unobligated allotments from implementing agencies, which are not savings within the contemplation of the Constitution; and (2) cross-border transfers of funds from the Executive to the Legislature and Judiciary. These acts contravene the constitutional principle that appropriations must be spent only for the specific purpose for which they were authorized.

title: Yuchengco v. Manila Chronicle Publishing
summary: The Supreme Court discussed the balance between press freedom and the right against defamation, establishing guidelines on the liability of media entities for libelous publications. The actual malice standard applies to public figures seeking damages.
doctrine: In cases involving public figures, the actual malice standard applies — the plaintiff must prove that the defamatory statement was made with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not. Press freedom does not grant absolute immunity from liability for defamation.
fullText:
VELASCO, JR., J.:

This case presents the tension between two constitutionally protected rights: freedom of the press and the right of individuals to their good name and reputation.

The freedom of the press is one of the cherished freedoms in a democratic society. However, this freedom is not without limits. The press must exercise its freedom responsibly and is accountable for its excesses.

For public figures, the actual malice standard governs liability for defamation. Under this standard, a public official or public figure may not recover damages for defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves that the statement was made with actual malice — that is, with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.

title: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the proper interpretation of tax exemption provisions, holding that tax exemptions are strictly construed against the taxpayer and liberally in favor of the taxing authority. The burden of proving entitlement to a tax exemption rests upon the taxpayer.
doctrine: Tax exemptions are construed strictissimi juris against the taxpayer and liberally in favor of the taxing authority. The taxpayer bears the burden of proving entitlement to any claimed tax exemption. When the tax code is clear, it must be applied as written.
fullText:
VITUG, J.:

The fundamental issue is whether the respondent is entitled to the claimed tax exemption under the National Internal Revenue Code.

It is a well-established principle in taxation that tax exemptions are to be construed in strictissimi juris against the taxpayer and liberally in favor of the taxing authority. Taxation is the rule; exemption is the exception. The burden of establishing a tax exemption is upon the taxpayer who claims it.

When the law itself does not make any exception in favor of any party, the courts may not create one. The language of the statute is clear and unambiguous. Tax statutes must be construed strictly against tax exemptions.

title: Chamber of Real Estate and Builders Associations v. Romulo
petitioner: Chamber of Real Estate and Builders Associations
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of the creditable withholding tax system on sales of real properties, ruling that it does not violate due process. The withholding tax system is merely a method of tax collection and does not impose a new tax.
doctrine: The withholding tax system is a procedure for collecting income tax at the source and does not constitute a new tax. It is a valid exercise of the taxing power and does not violate due process as long as the taxpayer can claim a credit for the withheld amount.
fullText:
CORONA, J.:

This case challenges the constitutionality of the creditable withholding tax system imposed on sales of real properties.

The withholding tax system was devised for three primary reasons: to provide the taxpayer a convenient manner of meeting his tax liability; to ensure the collection of tax; and to improve the government's cash flow. It is essentially a mode of collecting income tax in advance.

The system does not impose a new tax. It is merely a method of enforcing collection of an existing tax obligation. The taxpayer is not deprived of due process because the amount withheld is credited against the taxpayer's total income tax liability at the end of the taxable year.

title: Pangilinan v. COMELEC
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Overseas Absentee Voting Act, ruling that the right of suffrage extends to qualified Filipino citizens abroad. The law's mechanisms for absentee voting comply with constitutional requirements.
doctrine: The right of suffrage belongs to all qualified Filipino citizens, including those residing abroad. The Overseas Absentee Voting Act is a valid exercise of legislative power to implement the constitutional mandate of ensuring the right of overseas Filipinos to vote.
fullText:
NACHURA, J.:

The constitutionality of Republic Act No. 9189, the Overseas Absentee Voting Act of 2003, is the central issue in this case.

Section 1, Article V of the 1987 Constitution provides that suffrage may be exercised by all citizens of the Philippines. The Constitution does not limit the exercise of the right of suffrage to those actually residing in the Philippines. Congress, in enacting RA 9189, merely implemented the constitutional mandate to provide a system for absentee voting by qualified Filipinos abroad.

The law establishes sufficient safeguards to ensure the integrity of the electoral process while enabling overseas Filipinos to participate in the democratic exercise of choosing their leaders.

title: Technogas Philippines Manufacturing v. PNOC
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the measure of damages for breach of contract, holding that actual damages must be proven with reasonable certainty. Speculative or contingent damages cannot be awarded. The party claiming damages bears the burden of proving their existence and amount.
doctrine: Actual or compensatory damages must be proved with a reasonable degree of certainty. Courts cannot rely on speculation, conjecture, or guesswork in determining the amount of damages. The claimant must present the best evidence obtainable, such as receipts, invoices, or other documentary proof.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

The central question in this case is the proper measure and proof of damages arising from the breach of a supply contract.

Article 2199 of the Civil Code provides that actual or compensatory damages are those awarded in satisfaction of, or in recompense for, loss or injury sustained. Except as provided by law or by stipulation, one is entitled to an adequate compensation only for such pecuniary loss suffered by him as he has duly proved.

The amount of actual damages must be established with reasonable certainty, based upon competent proof and on the best evidence obtainable. Courts cannot simply rely on speculation, conjecture, or guesswork.

title: Association of Small Landowners v. Secretary of Agrarian Reform
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law (CARL), ruling that it is a valid exercise of the State's power of eminent domain. The law provides for just compensation to landowners and is consistent with the social justice provisions of the Constitution.
doctrine: The Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law is a valid exercise of the power of eminent domain for public use. Agrarian reform is a revolutionary measure that seeks to emancipate the tiller from the bondage of the soil. The determination of just compensation is a judicial function that cannot be limited by legislation.
fullText:
CRUZ, J.:

These consolidated cases challenge the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 6657, the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Law of 1988.

The agrarian reform program is founded on the right of farmers and regular farmworkers who are landless to own directly or collectively the lands they till. It is the policy of the State to pursue a Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program.

The power of eminent domain is inherent in every state. The CARL is an exercise of this power. The taking of private agricultural lands for distribution to farmer-beneficiaries is for a public purpose — social justice and equity. Just compensation shall be determined by the courts, which shall consider the cost of acquisition of the land, the current value of like properties, and other factors.

title: Intellectual Property Association v. Ochoa
petitioner: Intellectual Property Association of the Philippines
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the scope of patent protection in the Philippines, affirming the country's compliance with the TRIPS Agreement while recognizing the State's prerogative to balance intellectual property rights with public health and access to essential goods.
doctrine: Intellectual property rights are not absolute. They must be balanced against the public interest, particularly in matters of public health and access to essential commodities. The State may impose limitations on patent rights consistent with its obligations under the TRIPS Agreement.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

This case involves the proper interpretation of patent protection under Philippine law in the context of international trade obligations.

The Intellectual Property Code of the Philippines, Republic Act No. 8293, was enacted in compliance with the country's obligations under the TRIPS Agreement. However, intellectual property rights are not absolute. The State retains the sovereign prerogative to impose limitations on these rights in the interest of public welfare.

The TRIPS Agreement itself recognizes the right of member states to adopt measures necessary to protect public health and nutrition, and to promote the public interest in sectors of vital importance to their socio-economic and technological development.

title: Banco de Oro v. Equitable PCI Bank
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the liability of banks in cases of forged checks, holding that the drawee bank which pays on a forged check bears the loss, as it has the duty to verify the drawer's signature. The collecting bank may also be liable if it was negligent in accepting the check.
doctrine: A drawee bank which pays on a forged check is deemed to have made the payment on its own account and cannot charge the amount to the drawer's account. The drawee bank bears the ultimate loss for paying on a forged instrument, unless it can show that the collecting bank was negligent.
fullText:
NACHURA, J.:

This case involves the allocation of loss arising from the payment of forged checks between the drawee bank and the collecting bank.

Section 23 of the Negotiable Instruments Law provides that when a signature is forged, it is wholly inoperative, and no right to enforce payment thereof against any party thereto can be acquired through or under such signature. The forged signature is wholly inoperative.

The drawee bank, by accepting and paying the forged check, is deemed to have warranted that it verified the genuineness of the drawer's signature. Having failed to detect the forgery, the drawee bank must bear the loss. However, if the collecting bank was also negligent in its duty to ascertain the genuineness of the check, the loss may be apportioned.

title: Malayan Insurance v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the right of subrogation in insurance, holding that when an insurer pays for a loss, it is subrogated to the rights of the insured against the person who caused the loss. The insurer may then recover from the wrongdoer the amount it paid to the insured.
doctrine: Upon payment of the loss, the insurer is entitled to be subrogated pro tanto to any right of action which the insured may have against the third person whose negligence caused the loss. Subrogation is founded on principles of equity and is designed to prevent unjust enrichment.
fullText:
REGALADO, J.:

The principal issue is whether the insurer, having indemnified the insured for the loss of cargo, may exercise the right of subrogation against the carrier whose negligence caused the loss.

Article 2207 of the Civil Code provides that if the plaintiff's property has been insured, and he has received indemnity from the insurance company for the injury or loss arising out of the wrong or breach of contract, the insurance company shall be subrogated to the rights of the insured against the wrongdoer or the person who has violated the contract.

The right of subrogation springs from equity. It is designed to prevent double recovery by the insured and to permit the insurer to recover the amount it has paid from the party whose negligence caused the loss.

title: Pimentel v. Aguirre
summary: The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the withholding by the President of a portion of the internal revenue allotment (IRA) of local government units, ruling that the Constitution mandates the automatic release of the IRA and the President has no authority to withhold it.
doctrine: The internal revenue allotment of local government units must be automatically released. The President has no authority to withhold or reduce the IRA even in times of fiscal crisis. The fiscal autonomy of local government units is constitutionally guaranteed.
fullText:
PANGANIBAN, J.:

The issue before the Court is whether the President may, upon the advice of the Secretary of Finance, withhold a portion of the internal revenue allotment (IRA) of local government units.

Section 6, Article X of the Constitution mandates that local government units shall have a just share, as determined by law, in the national taxes which shall be automatically released to them. The key word is 'automatically,' which means that the release of the IRA requires no further action from anyone and cannot be withheld by any official.

The President cannot, even in the exercise of fiscal prudence or in response to an unmanageable public sector deficit, withhold a portion of the IRA. The Constitution is clear and leaves no room for interpretation.

title: Calalang v. Williams
summary: The Supreme Court upheld traffic regulations banning animal-drawn vehicles on certain Manila streets, defining social justice and affirming the broad scope of police power. The decision is notable for its classic definition of social justice.
doctrine: Social justice is neither communism, nor despotism, nor atomism, nor anarchy, but the humanization of laws and the equalization of social and economic forces by the State so that justice in its rational and objectively secular conception may at least be approximated. Police power is the most essential, insistent, and illimitable of all government powers.
fullText:
LAUREL, J.:

The question presented is the validity of Commonwealth Act No. 548 authorizing the Director of Public Works to promulgate rules and regulations for the regulation and control of the use of national roads.

Social justice is neither communism, nor despotism, nor atomism, nor anarchy, but the humanization of laws and the equalization of social and economic forces by the State so that justice in its rational and objectively secular conception may at least be approximated. Social justice means the promotion of the welfare of all the people, the adoption by the Government of measures calculated to insure economic stability of all the component elements of society.

The exercise of police power is valid if it is exercised in the interest of the public, and if the means employed are reasonably necessary for the accomplishment of the purpose and not unduly oppressive upon individuals.

title: Government of the Philippines v. Monte de Piedad
summary: In this early case, the Supreme Court ordered Monte de Piedad to return funds that were donated for earthquake victims but were instead used for the institution's own purposes. The Court held that money received for a specific charitable purpose must be used for that purpose.
doctrine: Funds received in trust for a specific charitable purpose must be applied to that purpose. The recipient cannot appropriate trust funds for its own use. The principle of solutio indebiti applies — if something is received when there is no right to demand it, the obligation to return it arises.
fullText:
TRENT, J.:

This case involves funds collected by the Spanish Government for the relief of victims of earthquakes in the Philippines which were deposited with the Monte de Piedad, a savings and loan institution.

The funds were donated by the people of Spain for a specific charitable purpose — the relief of earthquake victims. The Monte de Piedad received these funds in trust and had no right to use them for any other purpose.

When a person receives money or property which he has no right to retain, the obligation to return it arises. This is the principle of solutio indebiti. The Monte de Piedad must return the funds with interest, as it used money that belonged to others for its own benefit.

title: Abakada Guro Party List v. Purisima
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Expanded Value-Added Tax (E-VAT) Law, ruling that the grant of authority to the President to raise the VAT rate from 10% to 12% did not constitute an undue delegation of legislative power because Congress provided sufficient standards.
doctrine: The delegation of the power to fix VAT rates is valid when Congress provides sufficient standards and conditions for the exercise of the delegated authority. The completeness test and sufficient standard test are both satisfied when the law specifies the conditions triggering the rate increase.
fullText:
AUSTRIA-MARTINEZ, J.:

These consolidated petitions challenge the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 9337, the Expanded Value-Added Tax Law, which increased the VAT rate from 10% to 12%.

The petitioners contend that Section 4 of RA 9337, which authorizes the President to raise the VAT rate to 12% when certain conditions are met, constitutes an undue delegation of legislative power. The Court disagrees.

Two tests determine the validity of delegation of legislative power: the completeness test and the sufficient standard test. The completeness test requires that the law must be complete in all its terms and conditions when it leaves the legislature. The sufficient standard test requires that the law must offer a sufficient standard to specify the limits of the delegate's authority. RA 9337 satisfies both tests.

title: Lladoc v. Commissioner of Internal Revenue
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a donation to a religious organization is subject to donor's tax. The constitutional provision on tax exemption of religious institutions applies only to property taxes, not to income or donor's taxes.
doctrine: The constitutional tax exemption of religious institutions under Article VI, Section 28(3) of the 1987 Constitution extends only to property taxes, not to income, excise, or donor's taxes. A donation to a religious institution is subject to donor's tax under the Tax Code.
fullText:
PAREDES, J.:

The issue is whether the donation of a parish priest to his church is subject to the payment of donor's tax.

The constitutional provision exempting from taxation properties actually, directly, and exclusively used for religious purposes refers to property tax. It does not cover excise taxes, income taxes, or donor's taxes. The exemption is limited in scope and cannot be extended beyond what the Constitution provides.

Tax exemptions are strictly construed. The exemption from property tax enjoyed by religious institutions does not extend to other forms of taxation unless specifically provided by law.

title: Heirs of Malabanan v. Republic
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the requirements for judicial confirmation of imperfect title over alienable and disposable lands of the public domain, establishing the reclassification and possession requirements under the Property Registration Decree and the Public Land Act.
doctrine: All lands of the public domain belong to the State (Regalian Doctrine). For judicial confirmation of title, the applicant must prove that the land has been classified as alienable and disposable, and that the applicant or predecessors have been in open, continuous, exclusive, and notorious possession since June 12, 1945 or earlier.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

The central issue is whether the applicants have sufficiently proven their entitlement to judicial confirmation of imperfect title over the subject property.

The Regalian Doctrine dictates that all lands of the public domain belong to the State, and the State is the source of any asserted right to ownership of land. The applicant for land registration must establish that the land is alienable and disposable, and must present a positive act of the government declaring the land as alienable and disposable.

Section 14(1) of PD 1529 requires that the applicant must prove open, continuous, exclusive, and notorious possession and occupation of alienable and disposable lands of the public domain under a bona fide claim of ownership since June 12, 1945, or earlier.

title: Araneta v. Dinglasan
summary: The Supreme Court declared that emergency powers granted to the President during World War II ceased upon the adjournment of the Congress that granted them. The President cannot continue to exercise delegated emergency powers beyond the duration specified or implied by the granting legislature.
doctrine: Emergency powers delegated by Congress to the President are temporary and cease when the emergency that justified them ends or when Congress adjourns without renewing the delegation. The President cannot exercise emergency powers beyond their constitutional limits.
fullText:
TUASON, J.:

The question is whether the emergency powers granted to the President under Commonwealth Act No. 671 continued to be in force after the liberation of the Philippines and the convening of Congress.

Section 26 of Article VI of the 1935 Constitution provides that in times of war or other national emergency, the Congress may by law authorize the President to promulgate rules and regulations to carry out a declared national policy. The grant of emergency powers is extraordinary and temporary.

The emergency powers granted to the President must be deemed to have ceased when Congress convened in regular session. The delegation of legislative power to the President is temporary and must be construed strictly. Once the emergency ceases or Congress reassembles, the delegation expires.

title: People v. Vera
summary: The Supreme Court declared Act No. 4221 (the old Probation Law) unconstitutional for violating the equal protection clause. The law gave provincial boards the discretion to apply probation in their province, resulting in unequal application of the law across provinces.
doctrine: A law that leaves to the discretion of provincial authorities whether or not it will be operative in their respective provinces violates the equal protection clause. Laws must operate uniformly on all persons under similar circumstances.
fullText:
LAUREL, J.:

The constitutionality of Act No. 4221, known as the Probation Law, is challenged in this case on the ground that it violates the equal protection clause of the Constitution.

The Act provides that it shall apply only to those provinces where the respective provincial boards have appropriated funds for the salary of a probation officer. This results in a situation where persons convicted of the same offense in one province may avail of probation, while those in another province cannot.

The guaranty of equal protection of the laws means that no person or class of persons shall be deprived of the same protection of laws which is enjoyed by other persons or other classes in the same place and in like circumstances. The Probation Law, by making its application dependent on the action of provincial boards, creates an unreasonable classification.

title: Republic v. Sereno
summary: In a highly controversial decision, the Supreme Court granted a quo warranto petition against Chief Justice Sereno, declaring her appointment void for failure to file Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALNs). The decision was criticized for circumventing the impeachment process.
doctrine: A quo warranto petition may be filed against a member of the judiciary to challenge the validity of their appointment. The filing of SALNs is a legal requirement for appointment to a government position, and failure to comply renders the appointment voidable through quo warranto proceedings.
citedStatutes: RA 6713 (Code of Conduct for Public Officials)
fullText:
TIJAM, J.:

This is a petition for quo warranto filed by the Solicitor General against respondent Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno, questioning her qualification and eligibility to hold the position of Chief Justice of the Supreme Court.

The petition alleges that respondent failed to file her Statements of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth for several years prior to her application for the position of Chief Justice. The filing of SALNs is a legal requirement under Republic Act No. 6713.

The Court holds that a quo warranto proceeding is the proper remedy to question the eligibility of a person holding public office. The failure to file SALNs is not a mere procedural lapse but a violation of a substantive legal requirement that renders the appointment voidable.

title: Ang Ladlad LGBT Party v. COMELEC
summary: The Supreme Court reversed COMELEC's denial of Ang Ladlad's registration as a party-list organization representing the LGBT community. COMELEC's reliance on moral and religious grounds to deny registration violated the equal protection clause and the principle of non-establishment of religion.
doctrine: The COMELEC cannot deny a party-list organization's registration based on moral disapproval or religious beliefs. The equal protection clause prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation in the context of political participation. Moral disapproval, without more, is not a sufficient governmental interest to justify exclusion from the political process.
fullText:
DEL CASTILLO, J.:

This case involves the refusal by the Commission on Elections to register Ang Ladlad LGBT Party as a party-list organization on the ground of immorality.

The COMELEC cited the Bible and the Koran as basis for its denial, declaring that Ang Ladlad tolerates immorality which offends religious beliefs. This reasoning violates the non-establishment clause of the Constitution.

The equal protection clause guarantees that no person or class of persons shall be denied the same protection of laws enjoyed by other persons or classes in the same place and in like circumstances. Our Constitution provides in Article III, Section 1 that no person shall be deprived of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, nor shall any person be denied the equal protection of the laws.

title: Atong Paglaum v. COMELEC
summary: The Supreme Court overhauled the parameters for the party-list system, ruling that national and regional parties, not just marginalized and underrepresented groups, may participate. The decision broadened the party-list system while retaining protections for marginalized sectors.
doctrine: The party-list system is not exclusively for marginalized and underrepresented sectors. National and regional parties or organizations may participate. However, majority of the party-list seats should go to the marginalized and underrepresented. The party-list system was designed to democratize political power.
fullText:
CARPIO, J.:

These consolidated cases assail the resolutions of the COMELEC cancelling the registration of certain party-list groups for the 2013 elections.

The framers of the 1987 Constitution intended the party-list system to democratize political power by giving political parties that cannot win in legislative district elections a chance to win seats in the House of Representatives. The party-list system is not reserved exclusively for marginalized and underrepresented sectors.

The Court now holds that the following may participate in the party-list system: (1) national parties or organizations; (2) regional parties or organizations; and (3) sectoral parties or organizations. The major political parties may participate through their sectoral wings.

title: Bantay Republic Act v. COMELEC
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the right of citizens' arms to access election documents and the COMELEC's duty to ensure transparency in automated elections. The right to information on matters of public concern extends to election processes.
doctrine: The right to information on matters of public concern under Section 7, Article III of the Constitution includes access to official election records. COMELEC must ensure transparency in the conduct of elections, whether manual or automated.
fullText:
GARCIA, J.:

This case involves the right of citizens' arms to access election-related documents from the Commission on Elections in the context of automated elections.

Section 7, Article III of the Constitution provides that the right of the people to information on matters of public concern shall be recognized. Access to official records, and to documents, and papers pertaining to official acts, transactions, or decisions shall be afforded the citizen.

The conduct of elections is a matter of paramount public concern. The COMELEC has the constitutional duty to ensure free, orderly, honest, peaceful and credible elections. This duty includes making election processes transparent and accessible to public scrutiny.

title: Land Bank of the Philippines v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the determination of just compensation in agrarian reform cases is a judicial function. Courts are not bound by the formula prescribed by the Department of Agrarian Reform, though they must consider the factors enumerated in Section 17 of RA 6657.
doctrine: The determination of just compensation is a judicial function which cannot be limited by legislation or administrative regulation. While courts must consider the DAR formula, they are not bound by it. Just compensation must be the full and fair equivalent of the property taken from the owner.
fullText:
PANGANIBAN, J.:

The core issue is the proper determination of just compensation for lands acquired under the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program.

The determination of just compensation is a judicial function. The executive department or the legislature may make the initial determination, but when a party claims a violation of the guarantee against the taking without just compensation, no statute, decree, or executive order can mandate that its own determination shall prevail over the court's findings.

Section 17 of RA 6657 enumerates the factors to be considered in determining just compensation. While the courts should be guided by these factors, the ultimate determination of what constitutes just and fair compensation rests with the judiciary.

title: Department of Agrarian Reform v. Sarangani Agricultural Co.
