summary: The Supreme Court clarified the scope of CARP coverage, ruling that the reclassification of agricultural land to non-agricultural use prior to the effectivity of CARL exempts the land from agrarian reform coverage. The date of reclassification is the determinative factor.
doctrine: Lands reclassified from agricultural to non-agricultural use by the local government unit or by the DAR prior to June 15, 1988 are exempt from CARP coverage. The determinative factor is the date of reclassification, not the actual use of the land at the time of coverage.
fullText:
BERSAMIN, J.:

The issue is whether the subject property, which was reclassified from agricultural to non-agricultural use, falls within the coverage of the Comprehensive Agrarian Reform Program.

Section 4 of RA 6657 provides that the CARL shall cover all public and private agricultural lands. However, lands reclassified by proper government authority before the effectivity of the CARL on June 15, 1988 are exempt from CARP coverage.

The Court has consistently held that the reclassification of agricultural land to non-agricultural use before the effectivity of the CARL removes the land from its coverage. What determines whether a land is agricultural is its classification at the time of CARP coverage.

title: Coca-Cola Bottlers Philippines v. Agito
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the criteria for determining employer-employee relationships, applying the four-fold test. Workers who perform activities necessary and desirable to the usual business of the employer are considered regular employees regardless of the nomenclature of their contracts.
doctrine: The four-fold test determines the existence of an employer-employee relationship: (1) selection and engagement; (2) payment of wages; (3) power of dismissal; and (4) power of control. An employee who performs work necessary and desirable to the business is a regular employee under Article 280 of the Labor Code.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

The pivotal issue is whether the complainants are employees of Coca-Cola and, if so, whether they were illegally dismissed.

The existence of an employer-employee relationship is determined by the four-fold test: (1) the selection and engagement of the employee; (2) the payment of wages; (3) the power of dismissal; and (4) the employer's power to control the employee's conduct. The most important element is the employer's control of the employee's conduct.

Article 280 of the Labor Code provides that an employee who has been performing activities usually necessary or desirable in the usual business or trade of the employer shall be considered a regular employee. The law overrides stipulations in contracts that characterize regular employees as project or seasonal workers.

title: Jaka Food Processing v. Pacot
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the requirements for valid retrenchment under Article 283 of the Labor Code, ruling that the employer must prove actual or imminent substantial losses and that retrenchment is reasonably necessary to avert such losses.
doctrine: For a valid retrenchment, the employer must prove: (1) substantial and actual or imminent losses; (2) that retrenchment is reasonably necessary and likely to prevent the expected losses; (3) good faith; and (4) fair and reasonable criteria in selecting employees to be retrenched. The burden of proof rests on the employer.
fullText:
GARCIA, J.:

This case involves the legality of the retrenchment of several employees by the petitioner company on the ground of serious business losses.

Article 283 of the Labor Code authorizes the employer to terminate the employment of any employee due to retrenchment to prevent losses. However, the employer must prove that the losses are substantial, serious, actual and real, or if only expected, are reasonably imminent.

The employer must also show that it exercised good faith in implementing the retrenchment and that it used fair and reasonable criteria in ascertaining who would be dismissed and who would be retained. Mere allegations of projected losses without competent evidence are not sufficient.

title: Brent Hospital v. Zamora
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of fixed-term employment contracts, ruling that such contracts are not per se illegal provided they are entered into freely and voluntarily by the parties, with the period agreed upon knowingly and without force, duress, or improper pressure.
doctrine: Fixed-term employment contracts are valid when: (1) the period was agreed upon knowingly and voluntarily; (2) there was no force, duress, or improper pressure; and (3) the employer and employee dealt with each other on more or less equal terms. The decisive determinant is not the activities performed but the day certain agreed upon by the parties.
fullText:
NARVASA, J.:

The primary issue is the validity of a fixed-term or fixed-period employment contract.

The Labor Code does not proscribe or prohibit an employment contract with a fixed period. What it seeks to prevent is the circumvention of the right to security of tenure by the expedient of entering into successive short-term employment contracts.

Stipulations in employment contracts providing for term employment or fixed-period employment are valid when the period was agreed upon knowingly and voluntarily by the parties, without force, duress or improper pressure being brought to bear upon the employee and absent any other circumstances vitiating consent.

title: Manila Electric Company v. Benamira
summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between legitimate job contracting and labor-only contracting. Where the contractor merely supplies workers without substantial capital or investment and the workers perform activities directly related to the principal's business, a labor-only contracting arrangement exists.
doctrine: Labor-only contracting exists when: (1) the contractor does not have substantial capital or investment to actually perform the job; and (2) the workers recruited are performing activities directly related to the main business of the principal. In such cases, the principal is deemed the direct employer of the workers.
fullText:
CALLEJO, SR., J.:

The core issue is whether the arrangement between MERALCO and the contractor constitutes labor-only contracting, making MERALCO the direct employer of the workers.

Article 106 of the Labor Code defines labor-only contracting as an arrangement where the person supplying workers does not have substantial capital or investment in the form of tools, equipment, machineries, work premises, among others, and the workers recruited are performing activities which are directly related to the principal business of the employer.

In labor-only contracting, the law creates an employer-employee relationship between the principal and the workers. The contractor is merely an agent of the principal employer who is responsible to the workers in the same manner and extent as if the latter were directly employed by the principal.

title: Shangri-La International Hotel v. Developers Group
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the conflict between prior use and registration of trademarks. The Court held that in the Philippines, the trademark system follows the first-to-file rule under the IP Code, but prior use may still confer rights in certain circumstances.
doctrine: Under the Intellectual Property Code, the Philippines adopted the first-to-file system for trademark registration. However, a prior user in good faith may continue to use the mark within the area of actual use. Registration creates a prima facie presumption of ownership, but this may be rebutted by evidence of prior use.
fullText:
CARPIO MORALES, J.:

This case involves a trademark dispute between two entities claiming the right to use the 'Shangri-La' mark for hotel and resort services.

The Intellectual Property Code, Republic Act No. 8293, adopted the first-to-file system for the registration of trademarks. Under this system, the first person to file an application for registration of a trademark shall have the right to register the same.

However, the first-to-file rule does not completely disregard prior use. Section 138 of the IP Code provides that a certificate of registration is prima facie evidence of the validity of the registration, the registrant's ownership of the mark, and the registrant's exclusive right to use the same. This presumption, however, may be rebutted.

title: Pearl & Dean (Phil.) Corp. v. Shoemart
summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between copyright, patent, and trademark protections for advertising display units. A copyright over the engineering drawings does not extend to the actual physical product. To protect the product itself, a patent must be obtained.
doctrine: Copyright protection extends to the expression of an idea, not the idea itself. An engineering drawing may be copyrighted, but the copyright does not extend to the useful article depicted. To protect the physical product or industrial design, the proper remedy is a patent or industrial design registration.
fullText:
CORONA, J.:

The issue is whether a copyright over the technical drawings and intellectual creation of an advertising display unit gives the creator the exclusive right to manufacture and sell the display units themselves.

Copyright, in the strict sense of the term, is purely a statutory right. It is a right granted by a statute for the protection of literary, scholarly, scientific, and artistic works. A copyright protects the form of expression rather than the subject matter of the work.

There is a distinction between copyright and patent. Copyright covers the right to reproduce an original work, while patent protects the right to the useful invention. The copyright holder of technical drawings cannot prevent others from manufacturing the actual product depicted, unless a patent has been obtained.

title: Philippine National Bank v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court reaffirmed that the relationship between a bank and its depositor is one of creditor-debtor. Banks are required to exercise the highest degree of diligence in handling deposits and are liable for damages when they fail to return deposits on demand.
doctrine: The bank-depositor relationship is that of creditor and debtor. The bank has the obligation to return the deposit upon demand. Banks must exercise extraordinary diligence because of the fiduciary nature of banking. The degree of diligence required is more than that of a good father of a family.
fullText:
MELO, J.:

This case involves a claim by a depositor against the bank for the unauthorized withdrawal from the depositor's savings account.

The relationship between a bank and its depositors is that of creditor-debtor. The deposit under the account of the depositor creates a contractual obligation on the part of the bank to pay the depositor upon demand. The bank's failure to return the deposit upon demand constitutes a breach of this obligation.

The business of banking is imbued with public interest. The stability of banks depends on the confidence of the people in the honesty and efficiency of banks. Banks are required to exercise the highest degree of diligence in the selection and supervision of their employees and in the handling of their clients' accounts.

title: Bank of the Philippine Islands v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on criminal liability under the Trust Receipts Law, holding that failure to return the goods covered by a trust receipt or to deliver the proceeds of the sale constitutes estafa. The penal sanction applies regardless of good faith.
doctrine: Under PD 115 (Trust Receipts Law), the failure of the entrustee to account for the goods or their proceeds constitutes estafa under Article 315(1)(b) of the Revised Penal Code. The Trust Receipts Law is a valid exercise of police power intended to regulate trust receipt transactions and penalize dishonesty and abuse of confidence.
fullText:
YNARES-SANTIAGO, J.:

The issue is the criminal liability of the entrustee under the Trust Receipts Law for failure to account for goods covered by trust receipts.

Presidential Decree No. 115, the Trust Receipts Law, defines a trust receipt transaction as any transaction by and between a person referred to as the entruster, and another person referred to as the entrustee, whereby the entruster releases goods to the entrustee on the latter's execution of a trust receipt.

The entrustee is obligated to hold the goods in trust for the entruster, or to sell them and deliver the proceeds to the entruster, or to return the goods if unsold. The failure to comply with this obligation is punished as estafa. The penal provision is a valid exercise of the State's police power.

title: Sun Insurance Office v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that a fire insurance policy is a contract of indemnity where the insured can recover only to the extent of the pecuniary loss sustained. Over-insurance does not entitle the insured to recover more than the actual loss, and the insurance company may reduce recovery to actual value.
doctrine: A fire insurance contract is a contract of indemnity. The insured cannot recover more than the actual cash value of the property at the time of loss. The purpose of insurance is to indemnify the insured, not to enrich them. Over-insurance does not entitle the insured to profit from a loss.
fullText:
REGALADO, J.:

The issue is the proper measure of recovery under a fire insurance policy when the insured property is totally destroyed.

The Insurance Code provides that the measure of indemnity in property insurance is the extent to which the insured has been damaged. An insurer is not liable beyond the amount of the actual loss sustained by the insured. Fire insurance is a contract of indemnity — its purpose is to compensate the insured for loss actually sustained.

The insured cannot recover more than the actual cash value of the property at the time of loss, regardless of the face value of the policy. To allow otherwise would create a moral hazard and encourage arson.

title: White Gold Marine Services v. Pioneer Insurance
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that Protection and Indemnity (P&I) Clubs are engaged in insurance business and must comply with Philippine insurance regulations. A P&I Club provides marine insurance coverage against third-party claims and is thus subject to the Insurance Code.
doctrine: A Protection and Indemnity (P&I) Club is engaged in the insurance business within the meaning of the Insurance Code. Its operations in the Philippines require a license from the Insurance Commission. Any entity that assumes or distributes risk, whether or not for profit, is engaged in insurance business.
fullText:
CALLEJO, SR., J.:

The central issue is whether a Protection and Indemnity (P&I) Club is engaged in the insurance business in the Philippines and must obtain a license from the Insurance Commission.

Section 2(2) of the Insurance Code defines insurance as a contract whereby one undertakes for a consideration to indemnify another against loss, damage or liability arising from an unknown or contingent event. A P&I Club functions essentially as an insurer providing marine insurance coverage.

The test to determine if a contract is an insurance contract is whether the assumption of risk and indemnification of loss are its principal object and purpose. The P&I Club's undertaking to indemnify its members against third-party claims falls squarely within the definition of insurance.

title: Tan v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court laid down definitive rules on forum shopping, holding that filing multiple cases based on the same cause of action constitutes forum shopping. The submission of a certification of non-forum shopping is mandatory and its absence is ground for dismissal.
doctrine: Forum shopping exists when a party files multiple suits involving the same parties, causes of action, and reliefs sought. The certification against forum shopping is mandatory under the Rules of Court. Willful and deliberate forum shopping constitutes direct contempt of court and is a ground for summary dismissal.
fullText:
VITUG, J.:

This case addresses the evil of forum shopping which clogs the courts and threatens the orderly administration of justice.

Forum shopping is the institution of two or more actions involving the same parties for the same cause of action, either simultaneously or successively, on the supposition that one or the other court would make a favorable disposition. It is an act of malpractice as it trifles with the courts, abuses their processes, degrades the administration of justice, and adds to the already congested court dockets.

The test for determining forum shopping is whether the elements of litis pendentia are present or whether a final judgment in one case will amount to res judicata in the other.

title: Neypes v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court introduced the 'fresh period rule' in appeals, holding that a party who files a motion for reconsideration has a fresh 15-day period from receipt of the denial to file a notice of appeal. This standardized the period regardless of whether a motion for reconsideration was filed.
doctrine: A party litigant may file a notice of appeal within 15 days from receipt of the order denying the motion for reconsideration (fresh period rule). This fresh period applies regardless of the period already consumed before the filing of the motion for reconsideration.
fullText:
CORONA, J.:

The issue is the proper computation of the period within which to file a notice of appeal when a motion for reconsideration has been previously filed.

The Court standardizes the appeal period in this manner: a party litigant may either file his notice of appeal within 15 days from receipt of the Regional Trial Court's decision, or file it within 15 days from receipt of the order denying his motion for reconsideration.

The fresh period rule gives the party the full 15-day period from receipt of the denial of the motion for reconsideration within which to file the notice of appeal. This is consistent with the principle that rules of procedure should be liberally construed to promote their objective of securing a just, speedy and inexpensive disposition of every action.

title: Neri v. Senate Committee on Accountability
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the claim of executive privilege by NEDA Director General Neri, who refused to answer questions before the Senate regarding communications with President Arroyo about the NBN-ZTE deal. The presidential communications privilege covers advisory opinions given to the President.
doctrine: Executive privilege is constitutionally based and covers presidential communications. The presidential communications privilege applies to documents and communications that reflect the deliberative process of the President. However, this privilege is not absolute and may yield to the need for evidence in a criminal case.
fullText:
LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.:

This case involves the power of the Senate to compel the attendance and testimony of executive officials at legislative inquiries.

The presidential communications privilege is fundamental to the operation of government and inextricably rooted in the separation of powers under the Constitution. It applies to documents or other materials that reflect presidential decision-making and deliberations.

The elements of presidential communications privilege are: (1) the protected communication must relate to a quintessential and non-delegable presidential power; (2) the communication must be authored or solicited and received by a close advisor of the President; and (3) the communication must be made in the course of preparing advice for the President.

title: Republic v. Nolasco
summary: The Supreme Court abandoned the Molina guidelines for psychological incapacity cases, holding that the rigid application of these guidelines has led to unjust results. Expert testimony is no longer required, and the totality of evidence standard should be used.
doctrine: Psychological incapacity is not a medical or clinical concept but a legal one. The Molina guidelines are abandoned insofar as they require expert testimony and impose a rigid interpretation. Courts should assess the totality of evidence to determine if there is a durable aspect of personality that makes the spouse incapable of fulfilling essential marital obligations.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

This Court has been confronted with the question of whether it is time to revisit the guidelines set in Republic v. Court of Appeals (Molina) for the disposition of petitions for declaration of nullity of marriage based on psychological incapacity.

The rigid application of the Molina guidelines has resulted in the denial of relief to those genuinely trapped in marriages that are void from the beginning due to the psychological incapacity of one or both parties.

The Court now holds that psychological incapacity is a legal concept, not a medical one. It need not be proved through expert opinion. The totality of the evidence must show a durable or enduring aspect of a person's personality structure that manifests itself through clear acts of dysfunctionality that undermines the family.

title: Tuason v. Register of Deeds
respondent: Register of Deeds of Caloocan City
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the indefeasibility of a Torrens title, ruling that a certificate of title is conclusive evidence of ownership and cannot be collaterally attacked. The Torrens system was established to quiet title and guarantee the integrity of land titles.
doctrine: A Torrens certificate of title is indefeasible and imprescriptible. It cannot be altered, modified, or cancelled except in a direct proceeding. The purpose of the Torrens system is to guarantee the integrity of land titles and to protect the holder in good faith from any claim except those noted on the certificate.
fullText:
CONCEPCION, C.J.:

The central issue is the indefeasibility of a Torrens title registered under Act No. 496.

The Torrens system was adopted in the Philippines to quiet title to land and to put a stop forever to any question of the legality of the title. Once a title is registered under the Torrens system, the owner may rest secure, without the necessity of waiting in the portals of the court to avoid the possibility of losing his land.

A certificate of title serves as evidence of an indefeasible and incontrovertible title to the property in favor of the person whose name appears therein. After the expiration of one year from the issuance of the decree of registration, the title becomes conclusive and indefeasible.

title: Dumlao v. COMELEC
summary: The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the provision of BP 52 that imposed an additional qualification for candidates based on age (mandatory retirement), as it violated the equal protection clause by creating an irrational classification among elective officials.
doctrine: Additional qualifications for candidates for local elective positions beyond those prescribed by the Constitution and the Local Government Code violate the equal protection clause when they create unreasonable classifications. The legislature cannot impose qualifications that are not germane to the purpose of the law.
fullText:
MELENCIO-HERRERA, J.:

The constitutionality of the first paragraph of Section 4 of Batas Pambansa Blg. 52, which provides for an additional disqualification for elective local officials, is challenged in this case.

The provision disqualifies any retired elective provincial, city, or municipal official who has received retirement benefits and who is 65 years of age at the commencement of the term of office. The petitioner argues that this provision violates the equal protection clause.

The equal protection clause does not require universal applicability of laws. Classification is permissible provided it is based on substantial distinctions, is germane to the purpose of the law, applies to future conditions, and applies equally to all members of the same class. The classification in this case fails the test of reasonableness.

title: Ejercito v. Sandiganbayan
summary: The Supreme Court addressed procedural aspects of plunder cases before the Sandiganbayan, clarifying rules on bail, the right to speedy disposition of cases, and the scope of the Plunder Law in relation to the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.
doctrine: Plunder is a heinous crime and is not bailable when the evidence of guilt is strong. The right to speedy disposition of cases may be invoked when there is unreasonable delay in the proceedings. The Plunder Law is independent of the Anti-Graft Law and both may be applied simultaneously.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

This case involves various procedural issues in the prosecution of the plunder case before the Sandiganbayan.

Plunder, as defined in Republic Act No. 7080, is committed by any public officer who, by himself or in connivance with members of his family, relatives by affinity or consanguinity, business associates, subordinates, or other persons, amasses, accumulates or acquires ill-gotten wealth through a combination or series of overt criminal acts.

The right to bail is not absolute. Under the Constitution, bail is a matter of right only before conviction, except in cases where the offense charged is punishable by reclusion perpetua or death and the evidence of guilt is strong. Plunder, being a capital offense, requires a hearing to determine the strength of the evidence.

title: Ynot v. Intermediate Appellate Court
summary: The Supreme Court declared Executive Order 626-A unconstitutional for authorizing the summary confiscation of carabaos transported across provincial boundaries without due process. While the ban on carabao slaughter was valid, the confiscation penalty was an unreasonable and oppressive exercise of police power.
doctrine: While the State may validly exercise police power to regulate the slaughter and movement of carabaos, the outright confiscation of the animals without giving the owner a hearing violates procedural due process. The penalty must bear a reasonable relationship to the purpose of the regulation.
fullText:
CRUZ, J.:

The petitioner challenges the constitutionality of Executive Order No. 626-A which provides for the immediate confiscation of carabaos being transported from one province to another.

The police power is not unlimited. While the ban on the interprovincial transportation of carabaos may be a valid exercise of police power to preserve the work animals needed for agriculture, the penalty of confiscation without the benefit of a prior hearing is a denial of due process.

The due process clause applies to the exercise of police power. Even in the legitimate exercise of police power, the means employed must be reasonably necessary for the accomplishment of the purpose and must not be unduly oppressive upon individuals.

title: People v. De Joya
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the elements of self-defense as a justifying circumstance. When the accused invokes self-defense, the burden of proof shifts to the accused to prove by clear and convincing evidence the elements of unlawful aggression, reasonable necessity, and lack of sufficient provocation.
doctrine: Self-defense requires: (1) unlawful aggression by the victim; (2) reasonable necessity of the means employed to prevent or repel it; and (3) lack of sufficient provocation on the part of the person defending himself. Unlawful aggression is the indispensable element — without it, there is no self-defense.
fullText:
REGALADO, J.:

The accused invokes self-defense to justify the killing of the victim. When self-defense is invoked, the burden of proof shifts to the accused.

The essential elements of self-defense are: (1) unlawful aggression on the part of the victim; (2) reasonable necessity of the means employed to prevent or repel the aggression; and (3) lack of sufficient provocation on the part of the person making the defense.

Unlawful aggression is the most essential element. There can be no self-defense, whether complete or incomplete, unless the victim has committed unlawful aggression against the person defending himself.

title: People v. Sandiganbayan (Desierto)
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the discretion of the Ombudsman in finding probable cause for violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act. The Ombudsman's determination of probable cause is generally not subject to judicial review unless there is grave abuse of discretion.
doctrine: The determination of probable cause during preliminary investigation is an executive function. Courts generally do not interfere with the Ombudsman's exercise of this power unless there is a clear showing of grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction.
fullText:
CARPIO, J.:

The issue is whether the Sandiganbayan committed grave abuse of discretion in dismissing the information for violation of Section 3(e) of RA 3019.

The determination of probable cause during a preliminary investigation is an executive function. The Ombudsman is vested with the power to investigate and prosecute cases involving public officials. The Court has consistently held that it will not interfere with the Ombudsman's exercise of his investigatory and prosecutory powers absent a clear showing of grave abuse of discretion.

title: People v. Lol-lo and Saraw
summary: The Supreme Court convicted two Moro pirates of piracy, a crime against the law of nations. The Court held that piracy is a crime jure gentium (by the law of nations) and Philippine courts have jurisdiction over pirates regardless of the nationality of the victims or the location of the offense.
doctrine: Piracy is a crime against the law of nations (jure gentium). Any state may prosecute pirates regardless of nationality or where the crime was committed. Philippine courts have jurisdiction over piracy as an offense against the common law of all nations.
fullText:
MALCOLM, J.:

The accused are charged with the crime of piracy. On or about June 30, 1920, the accused, armed with bolos and krises, attacked two Dutch merchant vessels in Philippine waters, robbed the crew and passengers, and carried away two women.

Piracy is robbery or forcible depredation on the high seas, without authority and done with the intent to steal. It is a crime not against any particular state but against all mankind. It may be punished in the competent tribunal of any country where the offender may be found.

title: People v. Jugueta
summary: The Supreme Court laid down definitive guidelines on the amounts of damages to be awarded in criminal cases depending on the penalty imposed. This became the controlling case for standardizing civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages across criminal law.
doctrine: When the penalty imposed is death (reduced to reclusion perpetua): civil indemnity of P100,000, moral damages of P100,000, and exemplary damages of P100,000. When the penalty is reclusion perpetua: P75,000 each. When the penalty is reclusion temporal: P50,000 each. These amounts serve as guidelines for all criminal cases.
fullText:
PERALTA, J.:

This case provides an opportunity to lay down guidelines on the proper amounts of damages to be awarded in criminal cases.

The Court rationalizes the award of damages in criminal cases based on the penalty imposed. The amounts of civil indemnity, moral damages, and exemplary damages shall be determined by the severity of the crime and the penalty attached thereto.

These guidelines shall be applied prospectively and shall govern the award of damages in all criminal cases decided hereafter.

title: People v. Cabalquinto
summary: The Supreme Court established the rule that in cases involving violence against women and children, the identity of the victim and her immediate family shall be withheld and fictitious initials used. This was to protect the dignity and privacy of victims.
doctrine: In cases involving violence against women and children, the real name of the victim-survivor shall be withheld. Fictitious initials shall be used to represent the victim to protect her dignity and privacy. This rule applies to all stages of the proceedings and to all court issuances.
fullText:
PER CURIAM:

The Court takes this opportunity to address the need to protect the identity of victims of violence, particularly women and children.

Republic Act No. 7610, the Special Protection of Children Against Abuse, Exploitation and Discrimination Act, and RA 9262, the Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act, provide for the confidentiality of proceedings involving child victims.

The Court resolves that in cases involving violence against women and their children, the real name of the victim and her personal circumstances which tend to establish her identity shall be withheld. Fictitious initials shall be used to represent the victim.

title: West Tower Condominium Corporation v. First Philippine Industrial Corporation
summary: The Supreme Court issued a Writ of Kalikasan arising from a petroleum pipeline leak that contaminated the water supply of a residential condominium. The Court held that the writ is available when environmental damage is of such magnitude as to prejudice the life, health, or property of inhabitants in two or more cities or provinces.
doctrine: The Writ of Kalikasan is a remedy available when the environmental damage is of such magnitude as to prejudice the life, health, or property of inhabitants in two or more cities or provinces. The writ may issue even without a specific law providing for it, based on the constitutional right to a balanced and healthful ecology.
citedStatutes: Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases Rule 7
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

This case involves a petition for the issuance of a Writ of Kalikasan in connection with the leak from an underground petroleum pipeline that contaminated the water supply of a condominium complex.

The Writ of Kalikasan is an extraordinary remedy covering environmental damage of such magnitude that it prejudices the life, health, or property of inhabitants in two or more cities or provinces. It requires proof that the environmental law, rule, or regulation has been violated or will be violated.

The right to a balanced and healthful ecology is a self-executing constitutional provision that gives rise to a cause of action independent of any specific environmental statute.

title: Resident Marine Mammals of Tanon Strait v. Secretary Angelo Reyes
petitioner: Resident Marine Mammals of the Protected Seascape Tanon Strait
summary: The Supreme Court recognized the legal standing of marine mammals (through their stewards) to file a case protecting their habitat against oil exploration in a protected seascape. This expanded the concept of standing in environmental cases.
doctrine: Under the Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases, any Filipino citizen in representation of others, including minors and generations yet unborn, may file an action to enforce environmental rights. The liberal standing rule extends to environmental cases involving the protection of natural habitats.
citedStatutes: Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases Rule 2 Sec. 4
fullText:
LEONARDO-DE CASTRO, J.:

This unusual case presents the novel question of whether marine mammals, through their human stewards, have standing to sue for the protection of their habitat.

The Rules of Procedure for Environmental Cases provide for a liberal rule on standing. Under Section 4 of Rule 2, any Filipino citizen in representation of others, including minors and generations yet unborn, may file an action. The stewardship principle allows concerned citizens to file suit on behalf of the environment and its inhabitants.

The Court recognizes that environmental cases require a more liberal approach to standing, consistent with the constitutional policy of protecting and advancing the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology.

title: Segura v. Sandiganbayan
summary: The Supreme Court distinguished between evident bad faith and gross negligence under Section 3(e) of RA 3019. A conviction for violation of the Anti-Graft Law requires proof that the public officer acted with manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence.
doctrine: Section 3(e) of RA 3019 may be committed either by dolo (with evident bad faith or manifest partiality) or by culpa (through gross inexcusable negligence). The two modes are distinct and separate from each other. Evidence of evident bad faith requires proof of a palpably fraudulent and dishonest purpose.
fullText:
CARPIO, J.:

The issue is whether the petitioner is guilty of violating Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act.

Section 3(e) of RA 3019 punishes a public officer who causes any undue injury to any party or gives any private party any unwarranted benefits through manifest partiality, evident bad faith, or gross inexcusable negligence.

Evident bad faith connotes a palpably and patently fraudulent and dishonest purpose to do moral obliquity or conscious wrongdoing. It is different from gross inexcusable negligence which involves want of even slight care, acting or omitting to act in a situation where there is a duty to act.

title: Santos v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court first interpreted Article 36 of the Family Code on psychological incapacity, defining it as a mental incapacity that causes a party to be truly incognitive of the basic marital covenants. The incapacity must render the party unable to comply with essential marital obligations.
doctrine: Psychological incapacity under Article 36 refers to a serious psychological illness afflicting a party even before the celebration of marriage. It is not merely difficulty, refusal, or neglect in the performance of marital obligations. It must be a genuine psychic cause that renders the party incapable of understanding and complying with essential marital obligations.
fullText:
VITUG, J.:

This case presents the Court with the first opportunity to interpret Article 36 of the Family Code on psychological incapacity as a ground for declaring a marriage null and void.

Article 36 provides: 'A marriage contracted by any party who, at the time of the celebration, was psychologically incapacitated to comply with the essential marital obligations of marriage, shall likewise be void even if such incapacity becomes manifest only after its solemnization.'

Psychological incapacity must be characterized by gravity, antecedence, and incurability. It should refer to no less than a mental, not merely physical, incapacity that causes a party to be truly incognitive of the basic marital covenants.

title: Minucher v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the scope of diplomatic immunity, holding that a US Drug Enforcement Administration agent was immune from suit for acts performed in the course of his official duties. State immunity from suit extends to agents acting within the scope of their authority.
doctrine: Foreign agents performing acts within the scope of their official duties are immune from suit under the doctrine of state immunity. The immunity extends not only to the foreign state itself but to its agents and instrumentalities. The test is whether the act was performed in the discharge of official functions.
fullText:
VITUG, J.:

The central issue is whether a US Drug Enforcement Administration agent is immune from suit for acts performed in the course of his official duties in the Philippines.

The doctrine of state immunity provides that a sovereign state cannot be sued without its consent. This immunity extends to agents and instrumentalities of the foreign state when they act within the scope of their authority.

The test for determining whether a suit against a government agent is in fact a suit against the state is whether the ultimate liability will fall on the government. If the agent performed the act in the discharge of official functions, the suit is essentially one against the state and must be dismissed.

title: Southeast Asian Fisheries Development Center v. NLRC
petitioner: Southeast Asian Fisheries Development Center-Aquaculture Department
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that an international organization established by treaty enjoys immunity from suit. The SEAFDEC, as an international intergovernmental organization, is immune from judicial process and cannot be sued before Philippine courts without its consent.
doctrine: International organizations created by treaty enjoy immunity from legal process. This immunity is necessary to enable them to discharge their functions without interference from national courts. The immunity extends to labor disputes involving the organization's employees.
fullText:
FELICIANO, J.:

The issue is whether the Southeast Asian Fisheries Development Center, an international organization, enjoys immunity from suit before Philippine courts.

International organizations established by international agreements enjoy immunities from legal process. This immunity arises from the necessity to enable such organizations to discharge their functions effectively without interference from national courts.

The immunity of international organizations is well-established in international law. It is rooted in the same principles that underlie state immunity — the independence and equality of sovereign states.

title: Civil Service Commission v. Joson
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the power of the Civil Service Commission to directly discipline government employees. The CSC has original jurisdiction over cases involving presidential appointees and appellate jurisdiction over cases decided by departments and agencies.
doctrine: The Civil Service Commission has the power to hear and decide administrative cases against government employees. Due process in administrative cases requires notice and hearing but the rules of procedure are more relaxed than in judicial proceedings. Substantial evidence is sufficient for a finding of guilt.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

The question is the extent of the power of the Civil Service Commission to directly discipline government employees.

The Constitution vests in the Civil Service Commission the power to hear and decide administrative disciplinary cases involving civil service officers and employees. The CSC has original concurrent jurisdiction over disciplinary cases and appellate jurisdiction over cases decided by lower agencies.

Due process in administrative proceedings is not identical to due process in judicial proceedings. The essence of due process in administrative proceedings is the opportunity to explain one's side. Formal hearing is not always necessary.

title: Ang Tibay v. Court of Industrial Relations
summary: The Supreme Court laid down the cardinal requirements of due process in administrative proceedings. This landmark case established the standards that all administrative tribunals must observe to ensure fairness and impartiality in their proceedings.
doctrine: The seven cardinal rights of due process in administrative proceedings are: (1) the right to a hearing; (2) consideration of evidence presented; (3) decision based on evidence; (4) substantial evidence support; (5) independent consideration of evidence; (6) decision rendered in a manner that allows review; (7) decision based on the record or disclosed evidence.
fullText:
LAUREL, J.:

The Court takes this opportunity to lay down the cardinal primary requirements of due process in administrative proceedings.

(1) The right to a hearing, which includes the right to present evidence and arguments.
(2) The tribunal must consider the evidence presented.
(3) The decision must have something to support itself.
(4) The evidence must be substantial — such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.
(5) The decision must be rendered on the evidence presented at the hearing, or at least contained in the record and disclosed to the parties.
(6) The tribunal must act on its own independent consideration of the law and facts.
(7) The decision must be rendered in such a manner that the parties to the proceeding can know the various issues involved and the reasons for the decision.

title: Smart Communications v. Municipality of Malvar
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the taxing power of local government units over telecommunications companies, holding that LGUs may impose franchise taxes on businesses operating within their jurisdiction subject to the limitations prescribed by the Local Government Code.
doctrine: Local government units have the power to create their own sources of revenue and to impose taxes, fees, and charges, subject to the limitations prescribed by the Local Government Code. The taxing power of LGUs is broad but not unlimited — it must conform to the guidelines and limitations set by Congress.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

The issue is whether the Municipality of Malvar can impose a franchise tax on Smart Communications for its telecommunications operations within the municipality.

Section 5, Article X of the Constitution provides that each local government unit shall have the power to create its own sources of revenue and to levy taxes, fees, and charges. The Local Government Code, in Section 137, specifically empowers municipalities to impose a franchise tax.

However, the taxing power of local government units is not absolute. It is subject to the guidelines and limitations that Congress may provide.

title: Grave v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court discussed the hearsay rule and its exceptions in Philippine evidence law. A dying declaration, made under the consciousness of impending death, is admissible as an exception to the hearsay rule when the declarant subsequently dies.
doctrine: A dying declaration, to be admissible, requires: (1) the declaration concerns the cause and circumstances of the declarant's death; (2) it was made under consciousness of impending death; (3) the declarant was competent as a witness; and (4) the declaration is offered in a case involving the declarant's death.
fullText:
CALLEJO, SR., J.:

The issue involves the admissibility of an alleged dying declaration as an exception to the hearsay rule.

The hearsay rule provides that a witness can testify only to those facts which he knows of his personal knowledge. A dying declaration is an exception to this rule.

For a dying declaration to be admissible, the following requisites must concur: (1) the declaration must concern the cause and surrounding circumstances of the declarant's death; (2) at the time the declaration was made, the declarant must have been under the consciousness of an impending death; (3) the declarant must have been competent as a witness; and (4) the declaration must be offered in a criminal case for the death of the declarant.

title: Treyes v. Larlar
summary: The Supreme Court clarified the proper use of certiorari under Rule 65, holding that it is available only when a tribunal acts without or in excess of jurisdiction, or with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. It is not a substitute for a lost appeal.
doctrine: Certiorari under Rule 65 lies only when there is no appeal, or any plain, speedy, and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law. It is not a substitute for a lost appeal. Grave abuse of discretion implies such capricious and whimsical exercise of judgment as is equivalent to lack of jurisdiction.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

The issue is whether certiorari under Rule 65 is the proper remedy to assail the order of the trial court.

Section 1 of Rule 65 provides that when any tribunal, board, or officer exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions has acted without or in excess of its jurisdiction, or with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction, and there is no appeal, nor any plain, speedy, and adequate remedy in the ordinary course of law, a person aggrieved thereby may file a verified petition for certiorari.

Certiorari is not and cannot be made a substitute for an appeal where the latter remedy is available. Where the rules prescribe a specific remedy, certiorari is not the proper recourse.

title: Ko v. Philippine National Bank
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the right of redemption in extrajudicial foreclosure of real property mortgage. The mortgagor has one year from the date of registration of the certificate of sale within which to redeem the property.
doctrine: In extrajudicial foreclosure under Act No. 3135, the mortgagor has the right to redeem the foreclosed property within one year from the date of registration of the certificate of sale with the Register of Deeds. The redemption price includes the purchase price plus interest, assessments, and taxes.
fullText:
CARPIO MORALES, J.:

The issue is whether the petitioner validly exercised the right of redemption within the prescribed period.

In extrajudicial foreclosure of real property mortgage, the mortgagor has the right to redeem the property sold within one year from the date of registration of the sale with the Register of Deeds. This period is jurisdictional and non-extendible.

The redemption price includes the purchase price at the public auction, plus one percent monthly interest thereon, plus the amount of any assessments or taxes which the purchaser may have paid after purchase.

title: Spouses Arevalo v. Planters Development Bank
summary: The Supreme Court struck down an unconscionable interest rate imposed by a bank on a loan, ruling that while the Usury Law ceiling has been suspended, interest rates imposed must still be reasonable. Courts may reduce iniquitous or unconscionable interest rates.
doctrine: While the Usury Law has been effectively suspended by CB Circular No. 905, interest rates imposed on loans are still subject to the court's authority to reduce them when they are unconscionable. An interest rate of 36% per annum or higher is generally considered excessive and may be reduced by the courts.
fullText:
REYES, J.:

The core issue is whether the interest rate of 36% per annum imposed by the respondent bank on the loan is valid and enforceable.

While the Usury Law has been effectively repealed by Central Bank Circular No. 905, the Court has consistently held that this does not grant lenders unbridled authority to impose any rate of interest. The contractual stipulation on interest may still be struck down if it is unconscionable.

The Court has the authority to equitably reduce unreasonable interest rates. An interest rate that is excessive, unconscionable, or inequitable is void for being contrary to morals, if not against the law.

title: Nacar v. Gallery Frames
summary: The Supreme Court revised the guidelines on the imposition of legal interest rates, aligning them with BSP Circular No. 799 which reduced the legal interest rate from 12% to 6% per annum. This case became the controlling authority for the computation of legal interest in all money claims.
doctrine: Effective July 1, 2013, the legal interest rate for loans or forbearance of money is 6% per annum (previously 12%). For obligations not constituting a loan or forbearance of money, the rate is also 6% per annum. Once a judgment becomes final, the total amount shall earn interest at 6% per annum until full satisfaction.
fullText:
PERALTA, J.:

The Court takes this opportunity to settle, once and for all, the proper imposition of legal interest rates.

With the advent of BSP-MB Circular No. 799, effective July 1, 2013, the rate of interest for the loan or forbearance of any money, goods, or credits and the rate allowed in judgments, in the absence of an express contract as to such rate of interest, shall be six percent (6%) per annum.

The guidelines for the computation of legal interest are hereby modified as follows: (1) When the obligation is breached, and it consists in the payment of a sum of money, the interest due should be that which may have been stipulated in writing. (2) In the absence of stipulation, the rate of interest shall be 6% per annum.

title: Almeda v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court discussed the requirements and effects of adoption under the Domestic Adoption Act. Adoption creates a relationship of parent and child between the adopter and the adopted, and severs the parental authority of the biological parents.
doctrine: Adoption severs all legal ties between the biological parents and the adopted child, except in cases of succession rights to the biological parents. The adopted child is considered the legitimate child of the adopter for all intents and purposes. The best interest of the child is the paramount consideration in adoption proceedings.
fullText:
GARCIA, J.:

This case involves a petition for adoption under the Domestic Adoption Act of 1998, Republic Act No. 8552.

Adoption is a juridical act which creates between two persons a relationship similar to that which results from legitimate paternity and filiation. The adopted child is considered the legitimate child of the adopter for all intents and purposes.

The paramount consideration in adoption cases is the best interest of the child. The court must be satisfied that the adoption will redound to the best interest of the child and will provide a home and support that the child needs.

title: Republic v. De Gracia
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the requirements for a declaration of presumptive death of an absent spouse under Article 41 of the Family Code. The present spouse must prove a well-founded belief that the absent spouse is already dead, not merely absent.
doctrine: For a declaration of presumptive death, the present spouse must establish: (1) the absent spouse has been absent for four consecutive years or two years if there is danger of death; (2) the present spouse has a well-founded belief that the absent spouse is already dead; and (3) the present spouse files a summary proceeding for the declaration.
fullText:
CALLEJO, SR., J.:

The issue is whether the respondent has sufficiently established a well-founded belief that her absent husband is already dead to warrant a declaration of presumptive death.

Article 41 of the Family Code provides that a marriage contracted by any person during the subsistence of a previous marriage shall be null and void, unless the absent spouse has been absent for four consecutive years and the spouse present has a well-founded belief that the absent spouse is already dead.

A well-founded belief requires more than mere absence. The present spouse must show that he or she exerted reasonable and diligent efforts to locate the absent spouse.

title: Metropolitan Manila Development Authority v. Concerned Residents of Manila Bay
summary: The Supreme Court issued a continuing mandamus ordering government agencies to clean up and rehabilitate Manila Bay. The Court held that the government has a ministerial duty to enforce environmental laws and that citizens have the right to compel such enforcement.
doctrine: Government agencies tasked with environmental protection have a ministerial duty to enforce environmental laws. The right to a balanced and healthful ecology may be enforced through a writ of continuing mandamus. The Court may compel government agencies to perform their duties under environmental statutes.
fullText:
VELASCO, JR., J.:

The case involves a petition for mandamus to compel government agencies to clean up, rehabilitate, and preserve Manila Bay.

The Constitution guarantees the right of the people to a balanced and healthful ecology. Various environmental laws impose duties on government agencies to protect and preserve the country's water resources, including Manila Bay.

The Court issues a continuing mandamus directing the concerned government agencies to undertake the cleanup, rehabilitation, and preservation of Manila Bay. The continuing mandamus is warranted because the duty to protect the environment is a ministerial function that the government agencies are mandated by law to perform.

title: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. San Roque Power Corporation
summary: The Supreme Court laid down definitive rules on the prescriptive periods for filing judicial claims for VAT refunds. The 120-day period for the CIR to act on the administrative claim is mandatory and jurisdictional, and the 30-day period to appeal to the CTA is also jurisdictional.
doctrine: The 120+30 day periods for VAT refund claims are mandatory and jurisdictional. The taxpayer must wait for the lapse of the 120-day period before filing the judicial claim with the Court of Tax Appeals. Premature filing renders the petition without jurisdiction. The 30-day period to appeal is also jurisdictional.
fullText:
CARPIO, J.:

These consolidated cases present the issue of the proper interpretation of the prescriptive periods for filing judicial claims for refund of excess input VAT.

Section 112(C) of the NIRC provides that the Commissioner shall grant a refund or issue a tax credit certificate within one hundred twenty (120) days from the date of submission of complete documents. In case of full or partial denial, or failure to act within the 120-day period, the taxpayer may appeal to the Court of Tax Appeals within thirty (30) days.

The 120-day period is mandatory and jurisdictional. The taxpayer cannot file the judicial claim before the lapse of the 120-day period, as the CTA has no jurisdiction over premature petitions.

title: Commissioner of Internal Revenue v. Isabela Cultural Corporation
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the proper timing of tax deductions for accrual-basis taxpayers. Under the all-events test, an expense is deductible in the taxable year in which all events have occurred that establish the fact of the liability and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy.
doctrine: Under the accrual method of accounting, an expense is deductible for the taxable year in which all the events have occurred that establish the fact of the liability and the amount thereof can be determined with reasonable accuracy (all-events test). The actual payment of the expense is not determinative.
fullText:
YNARES-SANTIAGO, J.:

The issue is the proper taxable year in which certain expenses may be claimed as deductions by a taxpayer using the accrual method of accounting.

Under the accrual method of accounting, income is reportable when all the events have occurred that fix the taxpayer's right to receive the income, and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy. Similarly, an expense is deductible when all events have occurred that establish the fact of the liability and the amount can be determined with reasonable accuracy.

This is known as the all-events test. Under this test, it is the right to receive income or the fact of the liability — not the actual receipt of income or payment of expense — that determines the taxable year.

title: Azcuna v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the requirements for the probate of a will, holding that the probate court's role is limited to determining the due execution of the will and the testamentary capacity of the testator. Intrinsic validity of the will's provisions is examined only after probate.
doctrine: In probate proceedings, the court's authority is limited to determining: (1) whether the will was executed in accordance with the formalities prescribed by law; (2) whether the testator had testamentary capacity; and (3) whether the will was executed freely and voluntarily. The intrinsic validity of the provisions is not examined during probate.
fullText:
FRANCISCO, J.:

The issue is whether the lower court correctly disallowed the will offered for probate on the ground of undue influence.

In the probate of a will, the court's authority is limited to the extrinsic validity of the will — that is, whether the will was executed with the formalities required by law, whether the testator had testamentary capacity, and whether the will was executed free from force, duress, or undue influence.

The intrinsic validity of the testamentary provisions — such as the validity of the dispositions and the legality of the bequests — is to be passed upon only after the will has been admitted to probate.

title: People v. Sanchez
summary: Former Mayor Antonio Sanchez was convicted of rape with homicide for the deaths of Eileen Sarmenta and Allan Gomez. The Supreme Court affirmed the death penalty, ruling that the crime was attended by the aggravating circumstances of abuse of authority and use of a motor vehicle.
doctrine: When rape is committed and homicide results by reason or on the occasion thereof, the crime is the special complex crime of rape with homicide punishable by death. The use of position of authority to facilitate the commission of the crime is an aggravating circumstance.
fullText:
PER CURIAM:

This is an automatic review of the death sentence imposed on Mayor Antonio L. Sanchez for the crime of rape with homicide.

The evidence established that on June 28, 1993, the victims Eileen Sarmenta and Allan Gomez were abducted and brought to the Pasig River resort owned by Mayor Sanchez. Sarmenta was raped by the accused and his co-accused. Thereafter, both victims were killed.

The special complex crime of rape with homicide is punishable by death under Article 335 of the Revised Penal Code. The accused took advantage of his position as mayor to facilitate the commission of the crime.

title: People v. Pepino
summary: The Supreme Court acquitted the accused for violation of RA 9165 (Comprehensive Dangerous Drugs Act) due to the prosecution's failure to establish an unbroken chain of custody of the seized drugs. The integrity and evidentiary value of the corpus delicti were not preserved.
doctrine: In drug cases, the prosecution must establish an unbroken chain of custody of the seized drugs. Non-compliance with the chain of custody requirements under Section 21 of RA 9165 raises doubt on the integrity of the evidence and warrants acquittal. The corpus delicti must be preserved.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

The accused was charged with illegal sale and illegal possession of dangerous drugs under Sections 5 and 11 of RA 9165.

Section 21 of RA 9165 prescribes the procedure for the custody and disposition of confiscated drugs. The apprehending team must immediately conduct a physical inventory and photograph the seized items in the presence of the accused, a media representative, a DOJ representative, and an elected public official.

The failure to comply with these requirements, without justifiable grounds, casts doubt on the integrity and evidentiary value of the corpus delicti and constitutes a ground for acquittal.

title: People v. Lacanilao
summary: The Supreme Court discussed the sufficiency of circumstantial evidence to sustain a conviction. When there is no direct evidence, circumstantial evidence may be sufficient for conviction if there is more than one circumstance, the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven, and the combination produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt.
doctrine: Circumstantial evidence is sufficient for conviction when: (1) there is more than one circumstance; (2) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven; and (3) the combination of all the circumstances produces a conviction beyond reasonable doubt. The circumstances must constitute an unbroken chain leading to the conclusion that the accused committed the crime.
fullText:
VELASCO, JR., J.:

The issue is whether the circumstantial evidence presented by the prosecution is sufficient to sustain a conviction for robbery.

Direct evidence of the commission of a crime is not the only matrix wherefrom a trial court may draw its conclusion. Resort to circumstantial evidence is essential when direct evidence is not available.

Section 4, Rule 133 of the Rules of Court provides that circumstantial evidence is sufficient for conviction if: (a) there is more than one circumstance; (b) the facts from which the inferences are derived are proven; and (c) the combination of all the circumstances is such as to produce a conviction beyond reasonable doubt.

title: Heirs of Spouses Liwagon v. Heirs of Spouses Liwagon
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the effect of preterition (total omission of a compulsory heir in the will). Preterition annuls the institution of heir but does not affect devises and legacies insofar as they are not inofficious or excessive.
doctrine: Preterition or the total omission of a compulsory heir from the will annuls the institution of heir under Article 854 of the Civil Code. However, devises and legacies shall be valid insofar as they are not inofficious. The omitted heir is entitled to his legitime.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

The issue is the effect of preterition on the testamentary dispositions in the decedent's will.

Article 854 of the Civil Code provides that the preterition or omission of one, some, or all of the compulsory heirs in the direct line, whether living at the time of the execution of the will or born after the death of the testator, shall annul the institution of heir.

Preterition consists in the silence of the testator with regard to a compulsory heir, omitting him in the will. It differs from disinheritance in that preterition is merely an omission without an express exclusion.

title: Spouses Buenaventura v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court applied Article 1544 of the Civil Code on double sales, ruling that when the same immovable property is sold to different buyers, ownership goes to the buyer who first registers in good faith. Knowledge of a prior unregistered sale negates good faith.
doctrine: In a double sale of immovable property under Article 1544 of the Civil Code, ownership shall belong to the person who in good faith first recorded it in the Registry of Property. If there is no registration, ownership goes to the one who in good faith was first in possession. Good faith requires lack of knowledge of the prior sale.
fullText:
GARCIA, J.:

The issue is the resolution of a double sale of the same parcel of land in favor of two different buyers.

Article 1544 of the Civil Code governs the rule on double sale. It provides that should immovable property be sold to different vendees, the ownership shall belong to the person acquiring it who in good faith first recorded it in the Registry of Property.

Good faith in registration requires that the buyer has no knowledge of any defect in the title of the vendor or of facts which should put a reasonable person on inquiry. A buyer who registers a sale despite knowledge of a prior unregistered sale is not a buyer in good faith.

title: Macalinao v. Bank of the Philippine Islands
summary: The Supreme Court struck down the 3% monthly interest rate and other charges imposed by BPI on credit card balances as unconscionable. The Court reduced the interest to 1% per month and the penalty charge to 1% per month.
doctrine: Credit card interest rates are not exempt from judicial review. While the Usury Law ceiling has been lifted, courts may still reduce unconscionable interest rates on credit cards. A 3% monthly interest (36% per annum) on credit card balances is excessive and may be equitably reduced.
fullText:
PERALTA, J.:

The issue is whether the interest rate and penalty charges imposed by BPI on the credit card balance of the petitioner are valid and enforceable.

While the Usury Law has been effectively suspended, the Court has consistently held that interest rates imposed on obligations may be reduced when they are unconscionable. The 3% monthly interest rate (or 36% per annum) imposed by BPI is iniquitous and unconscionable.

The Court equitably reduces the monthly interest rate to 1% and the monthly penalty charge to 1%. Credit card agreements, being contracts of adhesion, are construed strictly against the party who drafted them.

title: Filipinas Life Assurance Company v. Pedroso
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the liability of an insurance company for the unauthorized acts of its agent. The insurer is liable when the agent's acts are within the apparent scope of authority and the insured relied on such authority in good faith.
doctrine: An insurance company is bound by the acts of its agents within the apparent scope of their authority. The doctrine of apparent authority or estoppel prevents the insurer from denying the authority of its agent when the insured relied on such authority in good faith.
fullText:
TINGA, J.:

The issue is whether Filipinas Life Assurance Company is liable for the unauthorized investment scheme of its agent.

The relationship between an insurance company and its agents is governed by the principles of agency. An agent can bind the principal only within the scope of actual or apparent authority.

The doctrine of apparent authority provides that where an insurance company, by its acts and conduct, holds out a person as an agent with authority to transact business, the company is bound by the acts of such person within the scope of apparent authority, even if the agent exceeded actual authority.

title: Spouses Decena v. Court of Appeals
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the security of tenure of agricultural tenants under the Agricultural Tenancy Act and the Agricultural Land Reform Code, ruling that tenants cannot be ejected except for causes provided by law and only after due process.
doctrine: Agricultural tenants are guaranteed security of tenure. No tenant shall be dispossessed of the landholding except for causes provided by law. The landlord-tenant relationship is not extinguished by the sale or transfer of the agricultural land. The rights and obligations of the agricultural tenant continue regardless of changes in ownership.
fullText:
NACHURA, J.:

The issue is whether the petitioners, as agricultural tenants, were validly ejected from the landholding.

The law guarantees security of tenure to agricultural tenants. Section 7 of RA 3844 provides that once an agricultural leasehold relation has been established, the tenant shall be entitled to security of tenure.

No tenant shall be dispossessed of the land he is cultivating except for causes authorized by law and only after due process. The transfer of the agricultural land to another person does not extinguish the agricultural leasehold relation.

title: Microsoft Corp. v. Maxicorp Inc.
summary: The Supreme Court ruled on the issuance of search warrants for software piracy, holding that the sale of counterfeit software constitutes a violation of the Intellectual Property Code. The Court upheld the validity of the search warrant issued based on probable cause.
doctrine: The unauthorized reproduction and sale of copyrighted software constitutes copyright infringement under the Intellectual Property Code. A search warrant may be issued upon a finding of probable cause that software piracy is being committed. The applicant must show that the copyrighted work is being reproduced without authority.
fullText:
CARPIO, J.:

The issue is the validity of the search warrant issued for the search and seizure of pirated Microsoft software from the premises of Maxicorp.

Copyright infringement consists in the unauthorized reproduction, distribution, or sale of copyrighted works. Section 177 of the Intellectual Property Code enumerates the economic rights of the copyright owner, including the right to reproduce the work.

A search warrant may be issued when there is probable cause to believe that copyright infringement is being committed. The unauthorized reproduction and sale of copyrighted software without license from the copyright owner constitutes a criminal offense under the IP Code.

title: Genuino v. De Lima
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that the DOJ Secretary has no inherent power to issue hold departure orders. Only courts have the authority to restrict a person's right to travel. The issuance of a hold departure order during preliminary investigation violates the constitutional right to travel.
doctrine: The right to travel may only be impaired by a court order, not by executive fiat. The DOJ Secretary has no authority to issue hold departure orders. Only a court, in the exercise of its judicial power, may restrict a person's right to travel through the issuance of a hold departure order.
fullText:
ABAD, J.:

The issue is whether the Secretary of Justice has the authority to issue hold departure orders against persons subject to preliminary investigation.

The right to travel is guaranteed by Section 6, Article III of the Constitution. It may only be impaired in the interest of national security, public safety, or public health, as may be provided by law.

The DOJ Secretary's power to issue hold departure orders has no constitutional or statutory basis. The restriction on a person's right to travel may only be imposed by a court of law. A hold departure order constitutes a restraint on liberty that requires judicial sanction.

title: Vivas v. Monetary Board of BSP
respondent: Monetary Board of the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the power of the Monetary Board to close and place a bank under receivership without prior notice and hearing. The close-now-hear-later doctrine applies to bank closures to protect depositors and the banking system.
doctrine: The Monetary Board may order the closure of a bank and place it under receivership without prior notice and hearing (close-now-hear-later doctrine). This is not a violation of due process because the bank has the remedy of filing a petition for certiorari to question the closure. The urgency of bank closures justifies summary action.
fullText:
BRION, J.:

The issue is whether the Monetary Board's order closing the petitioner bank and placing it under receivership without prior notice and hearing violates due process.

Section 30 of RA 7653 authorizes the Monetary Board to close a banking institution upon finding that it is unable to pay its liabilities as they become due, or that its continuance in business would involve probable loss to its depositors or creditors.

The close-now-hear-later doctrine has been upheld by the Court. The summary closure of a bank is justified by the urgent need to protect depositors and the stability of the banking system. The affected bank may question the closure through appropriate judicial proceedings.

title: Gatchalian v. Pavon
summary: The Supreme Court discussed the Rules of Procedure for Small Claims Cases, affirming that the simplified procedure is designed to provide an inexpensive, speedy, and accessible means of resolving money claims without the need for lawyers.
doctrine: The Rules of Procedure for Small Claims Cases provide a simplified and expeditious procedure for the resolution of small money claims. No attorneys shall be allowed to appear in behalf of or represent a party at the hearing. The rules are designed to promote access to justice for ordinary citizens.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

This case involves the application of the Rules of Procedure for Small Claims Cases.

The Supreme Court promulgated the Rules of Procedure for Small Claims Cases to provide a simplified, inexpensive, and speedy procedure for the recovery of money claims. The rules aim to make the courts more accessible to ordinary litigants.

Under the rules, no attorneys shall be allowed to appear in behalf of or represent a party at the hearing. The procedure is summary in nature and designed to dispense with the elaborate rules of evidence and procedure that characterize ordinary civil actions.

title: Hacienda Luisita Inc. v. Presidential Agrarian Reform Council
summary: The Supreme Court revoked the Stock Distribution Option Agreement (SDOA) of Hacienda Luisita and ordered the compulsory acquisition and distribution of the hacienda lands to qualified farmworker-beneficiaries. The SDOA was found to have failed in its purpose of benefiting the farmers.
doctrine: The Stock Distribution Option under Section 31 of RA 6657 requires that the farmworkers genuinely benefit from the arrangement. When the SDO fails to achieve its purpose and the farmworkers are not better off than they were before, the PARC may revoke the SDO and order compulsory land distribution.
fullText:
VELASCO, JR., J.:

The constitutionality and legality of the Stock Distribution Option Agreement of Hacienda Luisita is the central issue in this case.

Section 31 of RA 6657 provides an alternative to the outright transfer of land ownership through a stock distribution option where the farm workers receive shares of stock in the corporation that owns the land. However, this option is subject to the condition that the farmworkers must genuinely benefit from the arrangement.

The Court finds that the SDOA failed to achieve its purpose. The farmworkers did not receive fair benefits, and the stock distribution did not result in genuine agrarian reform. The PARC's order revoking the SDOA and directing compulsory land distribution is upheld.

title: Poe-Llamanzares v. COMELEC
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that foundlings are considered natural-born citizens of the Philippines, allowing Senator Grace Poe to run for president. The Court held that international law and the Constitution support the presumption that foundlings born in the Philippines are natural-born Filipino citizens.
doctrine: Foundlings are, as a class, natural-born citizens. There is no legal or constitutional basis to discriminate against foundlings as the Constitution does not deny foundlings the status of natural-born citizenship. International conventions and customary law support the presumption that foundlings found in a state are citizens of that state.
citedStatutes: UN Convention on the Rights of the Child
1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness
fullText:
PEREZ, J.:

The issue is whether petitioner Mary Grace Natividad S. Poe-Llamanzares, a foundling, is a natural-born citizen of the Philippines and therefore qualified to run for president.

Section 1, Article IV of the 1987 Constitution provides that citizens of the Philippines are those who are citizens at the time of the adoption of the Constitution, those whose fathers or mothers are citizens, those born before January 17, 1973, of Filipino mothers, and those who are naturalized.

The Court holds that foundlings are natural-born citizens. To hold otherwise would create a class of stateless persons and violate international conventions to which the Philippines is a signatory.

title: Calleja v. Executive Secretary
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020 in most of its provisions but declared certain provisions unconstitutional, including the designation power of the Anti-Terrorism Council and the penalty for publishing certain content.
doctrine: The Anti-Terrorism Act is constitutional in proscribing terrorism but certain provisions are unconstitutional. The designation of individuals as terrorists by the ATC without judicial authorization violates due process. Provisions penalizing those who publish content inciting terrorism are overbroad and violate freedom of expression.
fullText:
LEONEN, J.:

These consolidated petitions challenge the constitutionality of Republic Act No. 11479, the Anti-Terrorism Act of 2020.
