The law defines terrorism as engaging in acts intended to cause death, serious bodily injury, or extensive destruction or damage to property, government facilities, public utilities, or critical infrastructure when the purpose is to intimidate the general public, create an atmosphere of fear, or seriously destabilize the fundamental political, economic, or social structures of the country.

While the State has a compelling interest in combating terrorism, the means employed must not be overbroad or vague as to chill protected freedoms. Certain provisions of the law fail this test.

title: Province of Batangas v. Romulo
summary: The Supreme Court ordered the release of the full internal revenue allotment of local government units, striking down the practice of withholding portions of the IRA through executive issuances. The IRA must be automatically released in full without conditions.
doctrine: The internal revenue allotment is a constitutionally mandated share of LGUs in national taxes that must be automatically released without diminution. The President and the Secretary of Budget cannot impose conditions on the release of the IRA. LGUs have fiscal autonomy guaranteed by the Constitution.
fullText:
VELASCO, JR., J.:

The issue is whether the national government may withhold portions of the internal revenue allotment of local government units.

Section 6, Article X of the Constitution provides that local government units shall have a just share in the national taxes which shall be automatically released to them. The word 'automatically' means that the release should be immediate and without conditions.

The Court has consistently held that the IRA is a constitutionally mandated allocation that cannot be diminished, withheld, or subject to conditions imposed by the executive branch.

title: Republic v. Caguioa
summary: The Supreme Court ruled that reclaimed or foreshore lands belong to the State and are not susceptible of private appropriation. The Regalian Doctrine applies to all lands of the public domain, including those formed by natural accession along bodies of water.
doctrine: Foreshore and submerged lands belong to the State as part of the public domain. They are not registrable and cannot be the subject of private ownership. Reclaimed lands are also owned by the State and may only be disposed of through a law passed by Congress or through the applicable provisions of the Public Land Act.
fullText:
PERLAS-BERNABE, J.:

The issue is whether foreshore and reclaimed lands may be registered under the Torrens system in the name of a private individual.

The Regalian Doctrine provides that all lands of the public domain belong to the State. This includes foreshore lands, submerged lands, and reclaimed lands. These lands are inalienable and cannot be the subject of commerce or private appropriation.

The government, through the proper agencies, has the authority to reclaim lands from bodies of water. However, reclaimed lands remain part of the public domain and may only be disposed of in accordance with law.

title: Tiu v. Platinum Plans Philippines
summary: The Supreme Court upheld the validity of a non-compete clause in an employment contract, provided it is reasonable in terms of duration, geographical scope, and the nature of the restriction. The clause must be necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interest.
doctrine: Non-compete clauses in employment contracts are valid and enforceable provided they are: (1) reasonable as to duration and geographical scope; (2) necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests; and (3) not unduly oppressive on the employee's right to earn a livelihood. The restraint must be limited to what is reasonably necessary.
fullText:
NACHURA, J.:

The issue is the validity and enforceability of a non-compete clause in the employment contract between the petitioner and the respondent company.

The freedom to contract is both a constitutional and statutory right. Article 1306 of the Civil Code provides that the contracting parties may establish such stipulations, clauses, terms, and conditions as they may deem convenient, provided they are not contrary to law, morals, good customs, public order, or public policy.

A non-compete clause, while constituting a restraint on the employee's right to pursue a livelihood, is valid if it is reasonable and necessary to protect the employer's legitimate business interests.
